Vàng bước vào tuần mới sau một tuần giảm khá mạnh. Hợp đồng vàng Comex kết thúc tuần trước ở 4.133,7 USD/ounce, giảm 3,59% trong tuần và là tuần giảm thứ hai liên tiếp.
Giá vàng trải qua một tuần giảm mạnh khi lợi suất trái phiếu Mỹ và đồng USD tăng, trong khi kỳ vọng Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) tiếp tục duy trì chính sách tiền tệ thắt chặt gây sức ép lên kim loại quý, lấn át nhu cầu trú ẩn an toàn.
Giá vàng giao ngay khởi đầu tuần ở 4.277 USD/ounce, sau đó tăng nhẹ lên mức cao nhất tuần 4.280 USD/ounce. Áp lực bán gia tăng khi giá dầu tăng do căng thẳng Mỹ - Iran làm dấy lên lo ngại lạm phát, trong khi lợi suất trái phiếu kho bạc Mỹ kỳ hạn dài và đồng USD cùng đi lên.
Trong các phiên giữa tuần, giá vàng có thời điểm được hỗ trợ bởi dấu hiệu thị trường lao động Mỹ hạ nhiệt và niềm tin tiêu dùng suy yếu. Tuy nhiên, áp lực từ lợi suất trái phiếu và đồng USD khiến đà phục hồi không bền vững. Giá vàng sau đó giảm xuống mức thấp nhất tuần 4.110 USD/ounce.
Báo cáo việc làm mới nhất của Mỹ cho thấy nền kinh tế chỉ tạo thêm 29.000 việc làm trong tháng 9, trong khi tỷ lệ thất nghiệp tăng lên 4,2%. Số liệu việc làm của tháng 7 và tháng 8 cũng được điều chỉnh giảm. Những dữ liệu này khiến kỳ vọng Fed tăng lãi suất trong tháng 10 giảm, kéo đồng USD và lợi suất trái phiếu đi xuống.
Dù có thời điểm phục hồi, giá vàng vẫn không thể duy trì trên ngưỡng 4.200 USD/ounce. Áp lực bán gia tăng trở lại trong phiên cuối tuần, kéo giá kim loại quý đi xuống.
Chốt tuần, giá vàng giao ngay ở mức khoảng 4.141 USD/ounce. Giá vàng kỳ hạn tháng 11/2026 giao dịch quanh mức 4.172 USD/ounce.
Tuần này thị trường chú ý tới chỉ số PMI dịch vụ ISM tháng 9, biên bản họp Fed tháng 9, số đơn xin trợ cấp thất nghiệp và khảo sát tâm lý người tiêu dùng Michigan tháng 10.
Dự báo giá vàng
Marc Chandler, Giám đốc điều hành Bannockburn Global Forex, cho rằng việc lợi suất giảm sau báo cáo việc làm yếu của Mỹ đã tạo điều kiện để vàng phục hồi. Nếu giá vượt vùng 4.280-4.300 USD/ounce, thị trường sẽ có thêm cơ sở để tin rằng giá đã tạo đáy.
Adam Button, Trưởng bộ phận chiến lược tiền tệ tại investingLive, giữ quan điểm trung lập và cho rằng các nhịp điều chỉnh trong tháng 10 có thể tạo cơ hội mua trước khi bước vào giai đoạn thường có diễn biến tích cực từ tháng 11 đến tháng 1.
Adrian Day, Chủ tịch Adrian Day Asset Management, lại dự báo giá vàng có thể giảm trong ngắn hạn. Đà giảm khó kéo dài khi lợi suất và đồng USD hạ nhiệt, đặc biệt nếu Fed tạm dừng tăng lãi suất.
Rich Checkan, Chủ tịch kiêm Giám đốc điều hành Asset Strategies International, nghiêng về kịch bản giá vàng tăng, với kỳ vọng dữ liệu việc làm yếu và khả năng Fed không tăng lãi suất trong tháng 10 sẽ hỗ trợ kim loại quý.
Sean Lusk, đồng Giám đốc bộ phận phòng hộ thương mại tại Walsh Trading, cho rằng vàng đang gặp khó khăn trong việc duy trì đà tăng dù xuất hiện những yếu tố thuận lợi.
Tuy nhiên, yếu tố mùa vụ có thể hỗ trợ giá vàng trong tháng 10, với khả năng kim loại quý quay lại vùng 4.400-4.500 USD/ounce nếu đà phục hồi được củng cố.
Theo các chuyên gia, xu hướng giá vàng vẫn chưa rõ ràng. Vùng 4.200 USD/ounce là mốc quan trọng. Mức 4.280-4.300 USD/ounce được xem là vùng cần vượt qua để cải thiện triển vọng tăng giá.

articles.title: Etched fields funding offers at $40B+ valuation, sources say | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Although it’s only been a couple of months since Etched raised $700 million at a $21 billion valuation, the AI chip startup is already being plied with investment offers at double or more its value, according to people familiar with the company.
Etched is reviewing incoming bids that range from $40 billion from top-tier investors to $50 billion from lesser-known backers, one person said. These fundraising talks are early, so terms of any deal, should one happen, may change. Etched declined to comment.
While this may seem like a fast timetable to raise another mega round, Etched is pursuing a particularly expensive segment of the AI industry: building full AI hardware systems powered by its own proprietary chips. The person familiar with these offers said that if it raises as much as its last round, this could give Etched a cushion of as much as 3.5 years of runway.
There are reasons why VCs are hot to own a piece of Etched. The four-year-old startup shows promise of challenging Nvidia. Not only did quant trading firm Jane Street lead the last $700 million round, it is also a customer that took delivery of an early system. Etched said in July that it had already secured $1 billion in customer orders, including the one from Jane Street, after manufacturing its test chip at a TSMC factory this summer.
Co-founder and COO Robert Wachen previously told TechCrunch that investors are so enthusiastic because Etched has designed two new components from scratch to speed up inference — the computing process that happens after a user submits a prompt.
The company claims its chips can process more tokens faster and at a lower cost than Nvidia’s. That’s the reason its processors have been so attractive to Jane Street, for whom a microscopic advantage in speed can yield massive profits.
The startup has also impressed investors with its ability to attract engineers from Nvidia, with roughly 15% of Etched’s 400-person workforce having previously worked at the chip giant, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Etched also operates a new 10-megawatt data center in Silicon Valley and established a facility in Taiwan to coordinate production near TSMC.
Co-founders Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu famously met in an advanced math course at Harvard, while Wachen was Uberti’s roommate and they dropped out to pursue the company.
In terms of fast rounds at big leaps in valuations, Etched already has a history of them. The startup announced a $300 million round at a $10.3 billion valuation led by Sequoia in July. It announced the $700 million round at a $21 billion valuation in September. Back-to-back funding rounds, which essentially act as a single financing split into two tranches with separate valuations, are increasingly common among the buzziest startups.

articles.title: Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it? - Engadget
articles.text:
Are extended warranties on TVs and laptops ever really worth it?
Or are they just another useless upsell?
Have mercy on retail clerks. To keep their jobs, they're often asked to push promotions they know most customers don't want, such as memberships and credit cards. Upselling looks good on a manager's ledger, even if it irritates a good portion of their customers.
If you've been shopping for smart TVs, laptops or just about any major piece of electronics in the past decade, you've no doubt been pitched on the idea of an extended warranty, AppleCare+ and Best Buy Protection being a couple of familiar examples. At a glance, they're more reasonable than most in-store promotions. Everything breaks eventually, and the cost of some repairs can be eye-watering. Just ask anyone who's smashed the display on their MacBook.
Despite this, you can safely skip an extended warranty in most circumstances. They mostly exist for the sake of an upsell, which you can tell by the strings attached and the fundamental nature of consumer electronics. When an extended plan is justified, you'll likely know before you walk in the door.
Why extended warranties are usually a waste of money
For starters, extended warranties are typically focused around defects, and any TV, laptop or similarly expensive device is likely to be covered by the manufacturer for 90 days to a year or more. This matters because if a product is defective, it's going to fail under relatively normal strain, by definition. You're liable to find out quickly if it's faulty, though there are obviously outliers.
Another point is that while planned obsolescence is real, a product that survives the first year is likely to survive past the two- or three-year window that's common for many extended warranties. In an accelerated longevity test by RTINGS, 102 TVs were run nonstop between November 2022 and September 2025. Only two actually failed before they reached 3,000 hours, and most made it to at least 8,000. This longevity test employed TVs that had already been used for hundreds of hours, so the results didn't show an initial spike for models that failed right away — a spike that would be present if the TVs were all brand-new. But again, those failures often are covered by the manufacturer and wouldn't require an extended warranty. If you watched TV for four hours a day, every day, it would take you over two years to reach that 3,000-hour mark, by which point just 2 percent of the TVs had failed.
Unbiased reliability figures are harder to come by for laptops, but it almost doesn't matter for a couple of reasons. The first is that planned obsolescence factor. Within two or three years, just about any device you buy — especially a laptop — is going to be supplanted by something with improved performance for a similar price. Meanwhile, equivalent products are going to become cheaper and cheaper, especially if you're willing to buy a used or refurbished model.
That factors into the second point, which is the cost of an extended warranty vs. just saving up for a replacement or repair. To cover a $1,300 TV, for example, Best Buy charges approximately $160 for two years of Geek Squad TV Protection, and $280 for five years. While the cost of replacing the display panel could vastly exceed either sum, the retailer estimates that other repairs will typically fall between $255 and $395. You could spend most or all of the cost of a repair on a warranty you may never use, and you'll still be stuck with old hardware if you successfully pursue a claim.
Some warranties include loopholes, on that note. We can't make blanket statements, but it's important to watch out for clauses that prevent you from seeking repairs if there are signs of liquid exposure or anything else that could be branded user error, regardless of whether it's the source of your problems. In other situations, you may be forced to use a manufacturer's warranty first if it's still in effect, Geek Squad Protection being a prime example.
When does an extended warranty actually make sense?
Though TVs are rarely mission-critical, there are professionals who simply can't afford any downtime with a laptop or other productivity tools, and put the equipment they own through the wringer. The cost of an extended warranty is nothing by comparison, though if you're in this camp, it's essential that you pick a plan that allows for loaner units or rapid repairs or replacements. In fact, you may be looking at special business-oriented warranties that aren't pitched over the checkout counter.
If you hate the idea of downtime but you're not necessarily a professional, it can make sense to invest in a plan like AppleCare+. That incorporates theft and loss replacements for some devices and vastly reduced prices for fixing accidental damage, including liquids. Considering that many cities have an Apple Store or at least an authorized service site, same-day repairs and replacements are a real possibility.
Unfortunately, most vendors don't have such an extensive support network. If you need a repair, there's a strong chance your device is going to be shipped to a depot in another city, then back a few days later. And they may ship it back unrepaired if they can't replicate the issue you reported — something we've experienced directly. Every warranty is a gamble, in that respect.

articles.title: Giá bạc hồi phục, bạc thỏi có loại tăng gần 1 triệu đồng/kg
articles.text:
Tại thị trường trong nước, đầu phiên giao dịch hôm nay, giá bạc tại các doanh nghiệp kinh doanh bạc lớn được điều chỉnh tăng - giảm trái chiều.
Cụ thể, mở cửa phiên giao dịch hôm nay, Công ty CP Kim loại quý Ancarat điều chỉnh giá bạc miếng lên mức 2,132-2,198 triệu đồng/lượng (mua - bán), tăng 19.000 đồng/lượng ở cả chiều mua và bán so với mức chốt tuần qua.
Giá bạc thỏi của Ancarat cũng tăng 506.000 đồng/kg ở cả 2 chiều giao dịch so với kết tuần qua, niêm yết ở mức 56,853-58,613 triệu đồng/kg (mua - bán).
Cùng xu hướng, giá bạc miếng của Tập đoàn Vàng bạc Đá quý Phú Quý cũng tăng khá mạnh.
Giá bạc miếng của Phú Quý được niêm yết đầu phiên hôm nay ở mức 2,159-2,226 triệu đồng/lượng (mua - bán), tăng 33.000 đồng/lượng ở chiều mua và đắt hơn 34.000 đồng/lượng ở chiều bán so với mức chốt tuần qua.
Giá bạc thỏi của thương hiệu này mở cửa phiên hôm nay được giao dịch ở mức 57,573-59,359 triệu đồng/kg (mua - bán), tăng 880.000 đồng/kg ở chiều mua và đắt hơn 906.000 đồng/lượng ở chiều bán so với kết phiên giao dịch cuối tuần qua.
Trong khi đó, giá bạc tại Công ty TNHH MTV Vàng bạc Đá quý Ngân hàng Sài Gòn Thương Tín (Sacombank - SBJ) đầu phiên hôm nay được điều chỉnh đi xuống.
Mở cửa phiên hôm nay, giá bạc miếng tại Sacombank được niêm yết ở mức 2,139-2,211 triệu đồng/lượng (mua - bán), còn giá bạc thỏi của Sacombank được giao dịch ở mức 57,04-58,96 triệu đồng/kg (mua - bán). So với kết tuần qua, giá bạc miếng của Sacombank giảm 9.000 đồng/lượng trong khi giá bạc thỏi của thương hiệu này giảm 240.000 đồng/kg ở cả chiều mua và bán.
Trên thị trường quốc tế, mở cửa phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này, giá bạc được điều chỉnh đi lên.
Vào lúc 9h50' ngày 5/10 (giờ Việt Nam), giá bạc giao ngay trên thị trường thế giới được giao dịch ở mức 61 USD/ounce, tăng 1,22% so với phiên trước đó.
Mốc 61 USD/ounce đang trở thành vùng giá đáng chú ý với bạc. Việc bạc có thể giữ được vùng hỗ trợ này hay tiếp tục xuyên thủng sẽ có ý nghĩa quan trọng đối với tâm lý nhà đầu tư trong ngắn hạn.
Giá bạc tăng trở lại khi những kỳ vọng về khả năng Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) tăng lãi suất vào tháng 10 giảm xuống sau khi dữ liệu việc làm của Mỹ yếu hơn dự báo.
Tuy nhiên, xu hướng hồi phục trong ngắn hạn của giá bạc chưa rõ ràng, nhất là trong bối cảnh kim loại quý vẫn chịu áp lực từ lợi suất trái phiếu cao, đồng USD mạnh và rủi ro trên thị trường năng lượng.
Giới đầu tư đang theo dõi sát các số liệu CPI và PPI tháng 9 của Mỹ cùng với diễn biến giá năng lượng và những phát biểu mới từ các quan chức Fed trước cuộc họp chính sách vào cuối tháng 10.

articles.title: After Factory's public spat with Khosla, Menlo proudly invests | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy and his team announced Monday in a blog post that the firm has invested in AI coding startup Factory.
Menlo declined to comment on how much it invested but said the deal was part of Factory’s latest funding round announced last month at a $5 billion valuation. A source familiar with the deal told us the investment was significant to Menlo — not a token gesture — and that Menlo would have invested more had there been room on the cap table.
Ordinarily, something like this wouldn’t necessarily be news; startups often extend previous rounds to add new investors. But last week, Factory co-founder and CEO Matan Grinberg was embroiled in a very public airing of dirty laundry when he alleged that he had fired investor Chris Degnan of firm RPT Partners from his role as board advisor. Grinberg said he feared Degnan may have shared confidential information with Factory’s biggest competitor, Cognition. The accusation followed Degnan’s move to Cognition as its chief revenue officer.
A who’s who of the tech industry came out of the woodwork either to support Degnan and condemn Factory, or vice versa, but none was more surprising than Vinod Khosla. Khosla’s firm is an investor in both Factory and Cognition. But that didn’t stop the venerable VC from calling Factory a desperate “struggling second tier competitor,” and accusing Grinberg of lying about firing Degnan and impugning his character. Degnan disputed Grinberg’s story, saying he resigned and that he’d rebuffed a competing job offer from Grinberg.
So Menlo’s full-throated endorsement of Factory, which praised its founders, its tech, and its relationship with its customers, is more than a feather in Factory’s cap. It’s a statement that Factory is not in the state that Khosla implied it was.
Murphy famously bet his firm on Anthropic back when it appeared to be an also-ran to OpenAI and has been on a hot streak ever since, landing deals with Lovable and Legora, for instance. So now some VCs are calling Factory “the next Anthropic.“
Sequoia’s Shaun Maguire, also a Factory backer who came out on X in support of Grinberg last week, appears thrilled with Menlo’s endorsement, saying the firm is “on a tear.” Notably, Menlo is not an investor in competitor Cognition.

articles.title: Wikimedia links OpenAI agents to an outage and unauthorized activity - Engadget
articles.text:
Wikimedia links OpenAI agents to an outage and unauthorized activity
The foundation says it's "deeply concerned about the impact of 'rogue' AI agents on platforms like ours.
OpenAI agents have been running amok online, and it seems the Wikimedia Foundation has been affected too. The foundation says it detected unauthorized activity from OpenAI agents on its platforms, including edits to some wikis and failed attempts to compromise a note-taking tool. It reiterated that bots have been crawling data from its platforms en masse, while agents that appear to be operated by OpenAI have made millions of requests to its public APIs.
An investigation didn't turn up any evidence that AI agents were using Wikimedia systems to coordinate their activity (as they appear to have done on non-Wikimedia-operated wikis) and nor did the foundation detect signs of its data or systems being compromised. "However, we are concerned about what could have occurred here, the difficulty and effort involved in investigating and attributing this activity, and the growing risks of agentic AI activity on our platforms in general," Selena Deckelmann, the foundation's chief product and technology officer, wrote in a blog post. "The open web is a public good. We should not allow this behavior to become the 'new normal' for the people or organizations that maintain it." Engadget has contacted OpenAI for comment.
It appears OpenAI agents edited some Wikimedia wikis without permission. Almost all of these were test edits in sandbox sections of wikis and weren't visible on pages that users would generally access. There were also "a few edits to the configuration for a citation tool, which we believe were potentially malicious edits that were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services," Deckelmann wrote. While bots are permitted to edit Wikipedia under certain conditions, approval was not sought in these cases. (The English version of Wikipedia prohibits AI-generated articles.)
Moreover, agents that Wikimedia believes to stem from OpenAI attempted to compromise a note-taking tool called Etherpad, but those efforts failed. "Agents unsuccessfully tried to use it to fetch data from other websites as a proxy," Deckelmann wrote. "Other agents also likely operated by OpenAI took notes about their tasks, though this did not appear to turn into coordination."
The Wikimedia Foundation previously said that bots have been hammering its platforms since early 2024 to scrape data for generative AI training purposes. It now says agents have crawled millions of pages — mainly from Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons — and made "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to the Wikidata Query Service, which may have helped cause an outage in May.
"AI companies are not doing enough to secure their systems and protect the public from the harm they cause," Deckelmann argued, adding that Wikimedia is "deeply concerned" about the effect rogue AI agents can have on open knowledge platforms such as the ones it operates.
"Bots and agents are part of the future of the web, and the companies who unleash and profit from them must directly help avoid and repair damage they can do," Deckelmann wrote. "Our collective priority should be the health of the overall web ecosystem so that it continues to benefit all people — not just a handful of billionaires."
Wikimedia has offered a dataset for AI training purposes in an attempt to dissuade crawlers from scraping its platforms, which increases its costs and can potentially overload its systems. The foundation has also partnered with several tech companies to offer them streamlined access to data, but OpenAI isn't among them.

articles.title: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Reflection AI is officially unveiling Beam, its first frontier, open-weight AI model. The two-year-old, Brooklyn-based startup claims Beam matches the performance of leading Chinese open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks at dramatically lower costs, a claim that could heat up the race to build a Western answer to DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai.
Reflection’s announcement confirms reporting from Axios over the weekend that the startup was close to a launch. The company shared new details in a lengthy blog post Monday, which described Beam as a text-only mixture-of-experts model trained on high-compute reinforcement learning to be effective at reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks at “a fraction of the token cost and inference time compute” of rivals.
Beam is a 501-billion-parameter model with 23 billion active parameters. It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window. To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active.
Reflection’s performance claims haven’t been independently verified, but on advanced reasoning benchmarks, the company says Beam scores on par with Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and outperforms today’s leading Western open models while using “3-4x less inference compute.” Reflection calls it a “workhorse model” for enterprises, the public sector, and developers.
Reflection is positioning itself against closed labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, against popular open models from Chinese developers, and against Western players like Mistral, Meta, and Cohere. Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling, the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July. Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only.
Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook. Its last round valued the company at a $25 billion pre-money valuation.
The startup has also been locking up compute — a key ingredient needed to train frontier models capable of luring customers away from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s closed models, as well as the cheaper open-weight models from Chinese labs. This summer, Reflection signed deals collectively worth more than $7 billion with SpaceX and Nebius to secure access to Nvidia’s GB300 chips through 2029.
Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company backs Reflection, has long championed the “AI factory” idea and pushed to strengthen the open AI ecosystem — a vision that would also benefit Nvidia, whose GPUs would power those systems.
Axios reported that hedge funds and trading firms are among those eager to build such systems. Reflection has already begun testing the concept of a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea.
Reflection says it will release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month, with distribution through hyperscalers and neoclouds and integrations across open source libraries at launch.
Reflection did not respond in time to TechCrunch’s requests for more information.

articles.title: OpenAI will add a digital watermark to text and code generated in the EU - Engadget
articles.text:
OpenAI will add a digital watermark to text and code generated in the EU
This is to comply with the region's new AI transparency rules.
OpenAI just announced its plans to comply with part of the European Union's new AI transparency rules. The company will soon begin adding an invisible watermark to text and code generated in the EU. This follows a similar move by Anthropic earlier this year.
OpenAI is using a proprietary system called textGrain that "adds an invisible statistical signal to the model's word choices." Once added, a detector can spot these signals and ascertain if there's a watermark.
The company says the system "matched or exceeded" the performance of other approaches, like SynthID for text. However, it still cautions that "strong performance under ideal conditions does not guarantee reliable detection in everyday use."
That's corporate speak for "it may not always work." It admits that shorter text is harder to detect, with around an 80 percent success rate. The same goes for "content such as mathematics." Even editing text seems to bring down the success rate. OpenAI does plan on making the technology available in open source so others can tweak it.
The watermark will not be enabled by default, except for "eligible ChatGPT and Codex text output in the European Union." Customers will be able to opt-in "for select models," though it didn't specify which models would be available to the general global public.
OpenAI is being a bit more cautious when it comes to the detection software. Access will initially be limited to "approved researchers and expert organizations." Also, the detector doesn't identify the user or reveal prompts or conversations.
Article 50 of the EU's AI Act mandates that providers of generative AI systems make text outputs identifiable in a machine-readable way. This already pertains to new companies entering the market, but pre-existing entities have until December 2 to comply. This includes organizations like OpenAI and Anthropic, of course, but also Microsoft, Google and Meta, among others.

articles.title: Instinct brings its AI agent to group chats, even for friends without an account | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Instinct, the AI agent now valued at $10 billion as of its latest funding round, is expanding into group chats. The startup announced on Monday that users will be able to add the agent to chats with friends, which could be helpful in certain scenarios like travel planning, snagging event tickets, running fantasy leagues, organizing carpools, or managing who’s bringing what to Thanksgiving.
Notably, the group chats with the AI agent will work even if a user’s friends haven’t joined Instinct, the company said.
With the launch, Instinct moves ahead in its battle with top competitors in the space, like Meta’s Muse. The latter doesn’t yet offer the group chat functionality, though Meta’s older app, Meta AI, can be added to group chats on WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, and Facebook.
Instinct and Muse have been running neck and neck recently, with both of them adding the ability to make phone calls over the past couple of weeks, as their agents try to win more of the consumer AI market. Last week, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Dots, personal AI agents that can also be used in ChatGPT Spaces, collaborative workspaces where the Dots and humans work together.
On X, Instinct founder Noah Shinn explained how Instinct handles users’ privacy and security in group chats. He said a user’s personal Instinct agent will ask permission before connecting with the group’s Instinct agent, and that users can also choose which groups they trust and can remove that trust at any time.
Shinn also said the group’s Instinct is siloed from the users’ personal accounts, which it cannot access. The personal agent will always ask the user’s permission before sharing information or taking any action.
If new members join the group chat, any pending replies from a user’s personal Instinct agent are held before those are shared with the group, too.
“Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can explore options together, agree on a plan and get it done, all in one thread,” Shinn wrote.
The feature is rolling out initially to Instinct’s early access users but will expand to all users “soon.” To gain access to the new feature (or other recent additions), users can ask their Instinct agent to put them on the list to try it out.

articles.title: What is the purpose of a battery symbol next to a USB Port? - Engadget
articles.text:
What is the purpose of a battery symbol next to a USB Port?
Typically, it means faster charging speeds and bi-directional charging.
The more USB ports on a device, the better, but things can get confusing when they all have a different symbol on them. Among the markings seen next to USB ports, it's not uncommon to see a battery icon, which typically indicates that it's a USB Power Delivery port. Known as USB PD for short, this port means it can deliver higher power levels than a typical USB port, but can also charge connected devices.
The USB PD charging protocol has a long history and was first introduced in 2012, meaning it predates the debut of the USB-C port. However, USB PD was updated in 2021 and is now able to deliver up to 240W of power, meaning it can support more demanding devices like high-end laptops or some monitors. Beyond supplying more power, the USB PD port has some cool use cases that you might not know about.
What can you do with a USB port with a battery symbol?
When you see a battery symbol next to a USB port, it can mean a few things. Most commonly, the icon means that port is USB PD compatible and can offer a more sophisticated charging protocol. Using USB PD, you can charge your laptop faster since Power Delivery conducts an intelligent digital handshake between device and charger that provides the right amount of voltage and current without the risk of overheating.
The battery symbol could also translate to another useful feature in the form of bidirectional charging. When looking at your laptop's USB ports, you can use the one with a battery symbol to charge another device, like your smartphone or AirPods. Even further, some laptops' USB ports with this symbol can charge a device even when it's asleep or shut down thanks to "Always On" charging. Keep in mind that leaving your smartphone plugged into your laptop's compatible port can completely drain the battery. Luckily, most laptop makers have included a way to disable this charging feature.
Does a battery symbol always mean USB PD?
As much sense as a battery icon makes, USB PD has somewhat of an identity crisis when it comes to the symbol that represents it. According to the USB Implementers Forum, the nonprofit corporation that created and set the official USB standards, the official symbol is a battery shape made with negative space.
Members of the USB Implementers Forum include Apple, Microsoft and HP, but not all companies align with how they indicate that a USB port is equipped with the Power Delivery charging protocol. Across devices, there can be the official battery symbol from the USB Implementers Forum, a different battery logo, a lightning bolt (not to be confused with the Thunderbolt symbol) or even simply the letters "PD" to indicate that it's a USB PD port. On top of that, some companies will have USB ports that are compatible with the USB PD protocol but don't indicate it, like Apple's Thunderbolt ports for its MacBooks. If in doubt, it's best to check the manufacturer's specifications in a user manual.

articles.title: TikTok rolls out an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout | TechCrunch
articles.text:
TikTok announced Monday that it’s launching an AI shopping assistant and a new in-app checkout feature that lets users buy directly from brands.
TikTok describes its new Shopping Assistant as a conversational AI agent designed to help users discover and purchase products. The company says the assistant understands context and remembers users’ preferences and needs throughout the conversation. It offers real-time, AI-powered shopping guidance, such as product details, shipping information, sizing, availability, and help completing a purchase.
As for the new checkout feature, TikTok says users can buy directly from a brand from their For You feed (the app’s main, algorithm-driven video feed) with one click.
The new features could allow TikTok to capture more of users’ shopping journeys, and potentially more transaction value, without sending them elsewhere. By pairing a shopping assistant with direct payments, TikTok is turning its impulse-driven discovery feed into a place where users can get answers to questions about a product and make a purchase on the spot.
By building an AI assistant for shopping directly in its app, TikTok also appears to be hoping that users will stay within its platform when they have questions about a product, rather than turning to outside AI tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT.
The company says these new features are being built in partnership with commerce platforms and payment providers including Salesforce, Shopify, Shoplazza, and Stripe, among others.
While TikTok Shop, the app’s in-house marketplace, has been the platform’s main engine for the company’s e-commerce ambitions, these new features broaden its approach beyond the existing shopping hub. Rather than relying on TikTok Shop to drive purchases, the social network is now integrating shopping tools more directly into the broader app, including the For You feed.
The expansion comes as TikTok’s influence on shopping continues to grow. According to TikTok’s Economic Impact Report that was released last week, activity on the platform helped generate $81 billion in GDP for U.S. businesses, while 54 million Americans said they had purchased a product after watching a TikTok video.
TikTok Shop launched in the U.S. in September 2023. The market research firm eMarketer estimates it generated about $15.8 billion in U.S. sales in 2025, representing roughly 18% of all U.S. social commerce.

articles.title: Hyundai's all-electric hot hatch goes on sale in the UK, starting at around $25,000 - Engadget
articles.text:
Hyundai's all-electric hot hatch goes on sale in the UK, starting at around $25,000
The EV maker has no plans to bring the Ioniq 3 to the US, though.
Hyundai's Ioniq 3 and its extremely attractive price tag has landed in the UK. First introduced in April, the all-electric compact hatchback is now available to order, starting at £18,495, or around $25,000. That final price is thanks to a £3,750 Electric Car Grant in the UK that each Ioniq 3 model qualifies for.
Ashley Andrew, president of Hyundai Motor UK, said in a press release that the Ioniq 3 had more customers registering interest before launch than any other Hyundai introduced in the country. For that starting price, you get the Advance trim that's equipped with a 42 kWh battery and provides a 213-mile range. Alternatively, you can pay all the way up to £31,945, or around $42,000, for the top-end N-Line Evo version that comes with a 61 kWh battery and up to 308 miles of range. The Ioniq 3 was built on a 400V architecture, and it can charge from 10 to 80 percent in about 29 minutes (it might vary slightly depending on which size battery you choose).
Hyundai said the Ioniq 3 is its first vehicle in Europe to use its new Pleos Connect Infotainment system that's based on the Android Automotive OS and offers a more intuitive design. Depending on the trim, you can get either a 12.9-inch or 14.6-inch infotainment display, along with optional features like heated seats and steering wheel or Hyundai's smart driving features like Highway Driving Assist 2 and Blind View Monitor.
Hyundai describes the Ioniq 3 as an EV hatchback built for everyday European needs, so it's not surprising that it won't be coming to the US. On top of that, Hyundai's latest EV is being built in Turkey meaning that it would be subject to US tariffs that would take away from the main selling point of affordability. Instead, US customers have similar options with Hyundai's slightly larger Ioniq 5 or more recently, the Kia EV3 that starts at around $31,000.

articles.title: At 19, founder raises $11M for Ghost, maker of a $3,499 computer for personal AI | TechCrunch
articles.text:
For much of his life, Zain Javaid, 19, wanted to be a quant who uses math and data to guide his investment decisions. And for a while, he was one. But he got bored. Then, in 2022, ChatGPT was released, and he told TechCrunch, “I felt fundamentally excited in a way that I never had been before.”
He became interested in personal AI, and that interest led him to start Ghost, which announced Monday that it has emerged from stealth after a year of building, along with an $11 million seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz. Other investors in the round include Abstract, Audacious Ventures, SV Angel, and Nova. His founding team includes Nicholas Chua, 19, Yifei Chen, 24, and Gautam Sharda, 23.
Ghost’s first product is Core, a personal computer designed specifically for AI agents that can take actions on a person’s behalf. According to Javaid, the idea is to centralize a person’s data, from what’s on their desktop to apps to smart home devices, into one piece of hardware designed to continuously run AI agents that can act as an assistant, perform tasks, and understand a person’s life. “You can run models on existing hardware, but it’s a terrible experience on many levels,” said Javaid, who is also Core’s CEO.
Core includes an Nvidia RTX Pro 4000 SFF Blackwell GPU (a type of chip commonly used to run AI models), said Javaid, adding that the GPU is bundled into the device’s price, so customers don’t need to buy one separately. He said it also has its own software layer, browser, and filing system and can continuously process information and tasks without constant prompting. Core costs $3,499. Preorders for the first batch open Monday, and shipping is scheduled for the last week of October.
Javaid described Core as a “brain in a box” without a screen, which users access through a phone or app. Voice mode is also available, but users must speak into the Core app rather than the box itself. Core comes with three models preinstalled: Qwen-3.8-Next, Qwen-3.8-27B, and Gemma-4-31B.
Javaid said users can also install other models from Hugging Face, where developers share AI models, or load their own trained models. Asked how Core differs from a Mac Mini, Apple’s small desktop computer that some people set up to run AI tools, Javaid said Core’s hardware and software were built specifically for running AI agents, with models already installed, while the Mac Mini is a general-purpose computer that can be configured for AI.
“As new models or improvements to existing models come out, we can push out over-the-air updates, similar to how Tesla works,” Javaid said of Core, adding that if a new generation of models comes out, the company asks users whether they want to switch. “Users can also turn on auto-updates so they’re always running the latest generation of a given model.”
The team currently builds the units at its San Francisco facility. Javaid said the goal is to sell a fully functioning computer that doesn’t require complex setup or configuration. He said the models and personal memory run locally, and that all personal information is encrypted so that no cloud provider or third party, including Ghost, can meaningfully access it. He also said users can control how much autonomy they give their Core agents, and that the device is programmed to keep working if Ghost shuts down.
“All of the source code, logic, and model weights live on the device, not the services,” he said. “We build this device to not be dependent on having an outside entity maintaining the service.”
He said the team is also building a firewall to limit how the agent can use its credentials, such as logins and passwords. The firewall “monitors every outgoing network request on the computer and if it sees the agent performing a sanctioned action or exfiltrating data it shouldn’t, it rejects the request and flags it for user review.”
“The user owns all of it,” he said of the device, memory, and data. “Once you buy the hardware, everything is stored, run, and processed on the device.”
He said he is not too worried about the competition, including from established tech companies. “People sometimes give incumbents credit for having already built the product because they have the ingredients,” he said. He credited Apple with good hardware and disruption, but said much of what Core is aiming to tackle is software: “The model reasons over your life, how it remembers, how it takes action, how it knows when to reach out,” he continued.
Javaid offered an example of how Core is meant to work: “Core proactively sends you a notification that you might be getting sick because it sees your resting heart rate is elevated, sees from computer history that you were up late working on a project, and has seasonal context that it is flu season in San Francisco.”
The company’s main focus is building a product people love, he said. “If we can’t do that, Apple isn’t the reason we failed,” he said.
Above, Core’s founding team (L-R): Gautam Sharda, 23; Yifei Chen, 24; Zain Javaid, 19; and Nicholas Chua, 19.

articles.title: What are the limitations of using a USB-C to HDMI adapter? - Engadget
articles.text:
What are the limitations of using a USB-C to HDMI adapter?
An adapter can bridge the gap when your ports don't match, but you have to check for weak links along the chain.
Although USB-C cables are capable of high-speed data transfers and faster charging, the shift to them has created its own connectivity issues. If your laptop lacks an HDMI output and your display doesn't have a USB-C input, you might consider a USB-C to HDMI adapter for connecting your device to a TV, monitor or projector. While these adapters can help with mismatched ports, they aren't always a perfect solution. They might fail to send high-resolution video or simply display a blank screen.
These issues usually come down to the type of cables, ports and adapter you're using. Importantly, not all USB-C ports support video, with some only capable of charging your device and conducting data transfers. Moreover, the type of HDMI adapter and cable you use determines the maximum resolution and refresh rate of the output.
For permanent setups, top-rated USB-C hubs are often the best option. Or instead of an adapter, you might get a single USB-C to HDMI cable. The advice below will largely apply to all three options.
From USB-C to HDMI
Think of these connections as a relay, with your ports, cables and adapters all running the same signal between your device and display. Your device's USB-C port transmits a video signal through the HDMI adapter, where it is converted into an HDMI signal your display can read. Then, it's handed off to your HDMI cable, which carries it to the finish line of your TV or other display.
The quality of this connection is determined by the weakest link in the chain. With an incompatible port, old cable or overheating cheap adapter, the entire setup suffers.
Let's start with your USB-C port. USB-C ports can only carry video outputs if they support DisplayPort Alternate Mode, which uses the same DisplayPort digital display interface you might know from video cards. Which level of DP Alt Mode your USB-C supports impacts your video quality. DisplayPort 1.4 signals can reach 8K resolutions at a 60 Hz refresh rate, though 8K displays are so expensive that they're barely in use yet. DisplayPort 1.2 can achieve 4K resolution at 60Hz.
DP Alt Mode is an optional feature that manufacturers can add to standard USB-C ports. The Thunderbolt standard uses the same USB-C connection, but comes with guaranteed standards of data transfer rates (depending on the generation) and includes video output. Check the manual or online spec page to confirm a port's capabilities.
Even if your USB-C port can use DP Alt Mode, a basic USB-C charging cable won't transmit video signals; you need a fully-featured cable. If the receiving device doesn't have a USB-C port for video input, you'll need a specialized USB-C to HDMI cable adapter with a chip that converts your DP Alt Mode or Thunderbolt signal into an HDMI signal. The quality of this connection depends on the type of HDMI signal the cable and adapter are compatible with.
Ideally, your laptop will have at least two USB-C ports so you can charge with one while powering a display with the other.
A guide to HDMI signals
Not all HDMI signals are created equal. Since its introduction in 2002, the HDMI standard has gone through several iterations that each pack more bandwidth to allow for higher resolutions and faster refresh rates. Your connection will be limited to the oldest generation supported by either port, the cable or adapter.
While HDMI 2.2 has been approved, it's not really in use yet. Thus, the highest-quality option that's widely available is HDMI 2.1. Also known as Ultra High Speed, this generation of HDMI is more efficient than its earlier counterparts, capable of carrying up to 48 Gbps bandwidth. An HDMI 2.1 connection delivers 8K resolution at 60Hz and 4K resolution at 120Hz. Its other features include support for variable refresh rates, wider HDR signal compatibility and eARC support with enough audio punch to handle Dolby Atmos and DTS:X.
A tier lower are HDMI 2.0 cables and adapters. They're still capable of 4K resolution, albeit at a refresh rate of 60Hz. HDMI 2.0 adapters and cables should meet most streaming needs. The biggest limitation compared to its 2.1 successor is the noticeably lower bandwidth of 18 Gbps, making them not ideal for high-end gaming.
Avoid using earlier-gen HDMI adapters and cables, as they'll noticeably drop your signal quality below current standards. HDMI 1.4 can still reach 4K resolution, but at a diminished 30Hz refresh rate. Unless you've been holding onto a very old adapter, these won't be an issue.

articles.title: Hot Girl Hotline is like 'Dear Abby' for the AI era | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Women throughout history have always sought out relationship advice, whether from newspaper columnists like “Dear Abby,” letters to Cosmo, or just chatting with girlfriends. In the social media era, you can instead post anonymously on Reddit relationship forums or look to social media creators who discuss the topic.
Now, two sisters are launching a startup for young women, Hot Girl Hotline, which focuses on bringing AI into these conversations.
I know what you may be thinking: With all the advances in AI technology, founders are building something for women to talk about their dating woes? Well … yes!
The reality is that people have already been turning to large language models (LLMs) via apps like ChatGPT for this type of advice, and the team believes this type of activity should be handled more carefully.
Unfortunately, as we’ve seen, chatting with a general-purpose chatbot about personal topics can sometimes lead to disastrous effects — especially for those who were already mentally fragile. ChatGPT, for example, has faced a wave of lawsuits over its alleged manipulative conversation tactics that plaintiffs say contributed to negative mental health effects, including, in some cases, suicide.
The idea behind Hot Girl Hotline is to reach young women who are looking to have these sorts of private conversations while navigating dating life and relationships, but in a safer way.
“We’re not trying to be an AI companion,” explained Baila Mudgil, formerly a social media consultant, who co-founded the startup with her sister Sumrin (“Sumi”), who studied computer science at Stanford. “A companion is really going after solving loneliness, escapism, boredom — and you can rely on a lot of emotional dependency from that AI companion.”
Baila says the startup’s approach is to focus on offering quality advice grounded in behavioral science, but in a way that makes it feel like you’re chatting with a trusted friend or big sister. The conversation is often Socratic, with the AI asking you questions to help you arrive at the answer yourself.
“This is not to replace speaking to a human. This is not clinical advice, and we have a lot of safeguards in place … we take safety really seriously,” Baila said. If conversations raise flags, for instance, the user is referred to resources such as the crisis hotline 988.
“We believe the key to quality advice is not just knowing what to do next; it’s understanding why you’re doing it. So that’s a big piece of it,” added Sumi.
Notably, the AI also knows when to end the conversation; it doesn’t keep asking follow-up questions to drag you further down a rabbit hole. Instead, it pushes users to go take action out in the real world rather than ruminate on the problem.
The sisters believe there’s room for an app like this because not everyone wants to post on the web for advice, and there are times when you don’t want to bring up a personal, dating, or relationship-focused issue with a friend.
Friends can bring their own biases into the conversation, or the user may not want to put their partner on blast for something they did before they determine whether they’re going to work through it or end the relationship.
“It doesn’t mean you’re replacing your friend — you’re just trying to get another perspective,” says Baila of the hotline.
The app also personalizes its advice for each user to reflect their values, goals, identity, and tastes.
Under the hood, the startup relies on a mix of AI models and encrypts users’ data in transit and at rest. It doesn’t sell or train on the data, either. When it uses a third-party AI model, it follows a zero-data-retention policy there as well.
Hot Girl Hotline plans to monetize through a $9.99 per month subscription, which hundreds of its most active users are already paying for. Later, it may incorporate ads, too.
Relationship advice is just the beginning of how the company wants to cater to young women. It also plans to expand into other areas, like beauty and lifestyle.
New York-based Hot Girl Hotline is currently bootstrapped and will be participating in the Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco. It’s available on iOS and the web.

articles.title: Here's why it's important to keep your phone apps updated - Engadget
articles.text:
Here's why it's important to keep your phone apps updated
Those update alerts aren’t just there to annoy you.
You're likely nagged to update something every day, whether it's an OS, browser, console game or anything else with an internet connection. Apps on your phone might seem like a minor update in the grand scheme, but you shouldn't let them sit forever. Updating apps has lots of benefits, and delaying them for too long can cause problems.
Thankfully, this isn't as much of an issue since automatic updates are a quick toggle in the App Store (Settings > Apps > App Store > App Updates) or Google Play Store (in the app, tap your profile picture, then go to Settings > Network Preferences > Auto-update apps).
But you shouldn't fully rely on them, either. Updates can get stuck or fail, like when you have to manually update Android Auto. And they don't necessarily reach your device as soon as they're available. It's best to pair auto-updates with manual checks every so often to make sure they're running as they should. And when those updates are installed, you should know what's happening behind the scenes.
New features
This is the most obvious change when you update an app: buttons moved, features added or libraries expanded. We've all had the experience of opening one of our favorite apps and being surprised by its new look. Some apps, like social media, change constantly. Others, like those for shopping or utilities, might only change once or twice a year.
If you skip updates, you'll miss new tools like leaving notes on Spotify songs, smarter playback options in a podcast app, new courses in Duolingo and fresh tracks in the Nintendo Music app. While the changes that matter most to you depend on which apps you use, you won't want to miss out on your favorites being able to offer more.
This is one of the items that comes with drawbacks, though. App updates can take functionality away or break what once worked fine. You also might simply not prefer an app's new setup compared to how it used to be. Thankfully, developers of active apps should be quick to fix widespread issues, and after using the new version for a while, you'll acclimate again.
Security improvements
Patching security vulnerabilities is the biggest reason to update apps even when you don't feel like it. While not as crucial as OS vulnerabilities, security flaws in apps could potentially open up your device or information within the app to attack. This is more of a concern on Android than iPhone, since iOS isolates apps more strictly.
However, there have historically been attacks that abuse iPhone apps, like making calls without your permission. And earlier in 2026, an exploit was discovered in Zoom's apps that let you take control of other people's devices. It's not as if every app is terribly vulnerable the second you're running an older version, but you never know when something you use could become the next target.
The longer a security issue is known about, the more time attackers have to craft an exploit plan. Installing the latest patches and fixing the issue means your device won't be in their sights once nefarious folks figure out how to cause damage.
Compatibility, bug fixes and better performance
Aside from brand-new functionality, updates can bring performance enhancements to existing apps. Developers might simplify the codebase to streamline performance, fix bugs that caused crashes or make the app easier on battery. They might find ways to perform the same tasks without being as stressful on the hardware. These are small tweaks you might not notice at first, but make your overall experience smoother.
While not as frequent, OS compatibility is also a reason for app updates. When a new version of Android or iOS is coming, developers need to make sure their app runs on it properly. If you update your OS but not apps, they could run into trouble. This ties back into new features, too. For example, when Uber added Live Activities to its iOS app, you wouldn't see them until you installed the latest version.
In some cases, apps might refuse to run until you install the latest version. This can happen at an inopportune time, like if you've just gotten on a plane and won't have an internet connection for a while. Updating regularly avoids your favorite app not working when you're in the middle of a camping trip with no signal.

articles.title: 5 startups that caught VCs' attention at the latest PearX demo day | TechCrunch
articles.text:
There isn’t a shortage of accelerators for startups, but one of the few that investors watch closely is PearX, a 12-week program that caps its cohorts at a mere 20 startups and is run by Pear VC, a pre-seed and seed-focused venture firm.
PearX’s biannual demo day is consistently attended by top venture capitalists, reflecting the historically strong caliber of companies in each batch. Some of the startups that came out of recent cohorts include Known, which uses voice AI to match people for dates and secured funding from Forerunner Ventures. Another is Andera, a startup that automates corporate audit and compliance tasks and raised a $37 million Series A from Lightspeed this summer.
The PearX program distinguishes itself from Y Combinator, the OG of startup accelerators, in several ways. Besides being much smaller, it doesn’t offer companies standard terms. Its investments can be as high as $2 million. Moreover, unlike YC, where some of the buzziest startups raise funding before the program ends, PearX claims to keep its participants under wraps until demo day.
TechCrunch attended Pear’s latest demo day, which took place in San Francisco last week, and then stuck around to ask some of the VCs about which companies stood out to them out of the 16 startups in the batch.
Below are five of the companies that seemed to have generated the most buzz.
Speridlabs
What it does: Spatial foundational models for powering robotics, gaming, and special effects.
Why it stood out: While Speridlabs is certainly not the only startup developing world models to do for 3D space what LLMs did for language, it argues that its more established competitors, including Runway, Odyssey, and Google’s Genie, cannot be queried or modified. To solve this, Speridlabs built Mundus, which it calls a 3D Midjourney because it keeps its geometry persistent when a part is changed.
Saia
What it does: Builds a fast, cost-efficient chip that runs inference directly on device.
Why it stood out: Nvidia’s GPUs and Google’s TPUs require expensive, power-hungry memory that is currently in short supply. Saia claims to have designed a chip that bypasses traditional memory by running AI directly out of flash storage. The startup claims its chip delivers vastly superior speeds and eight times the capacity while using four times less power than Nvidia’s Jetson, a leading local AI chip and board. Saia says it’s already in discussions with Samsung regarding memory integration, plans to start fabricating test chips next year, and aims to launch mass production by 2028. Developing hardware is notoriously brutal, but 20-year-old founder Ayaan Govil managed to convince Pear VC co-founder Mar Hershenson, a semiconductor engineer with a PhD in circuit design, to take a chance on his vision.
Ren
What it does: A more secure AI personal assistant.
Why it stood out: Ren claims to offer functionality similar to Muse and Instinct, but with a heavy focus on security and privacy. The startup says it keeps data on-device where possible or uses a secure private cloud, checking actions against strict user-set guardrails. Furthermore, Ren distinguishes itself from competitors that rely on human operators to place phone calls by using a fully automated voice system, keeping human involvement entirely out of the loop to protect user privacy.
Veros
What it does: AI native trust and estate planner.
Why it stood out: Setting up a trust is expensive and time-consuming. Veros wants to simplify the work normally done by attorneys, wealth managers, and trust administrators by employing AI to recommend structures and manage assets over their lifetime. Already managing $250 million in AUM, the startup is also in the process of securing a trust charter so it can operate as a regulated trust company itself.
Datum
What it does: AI engineer for industrial design.
Why it stood out: Datum wants to expedite physical product development by helping engineers find and use what they built previously. The startup indexes a company’s library of 3D designs. Using proprietary Geometric Fingerprint technology, Datum identifies parts based on their shape, helping streamline and automate engineering across a massive physical design market.

articles.title: How to turn on Developer Mode on your Chromebook - Engadget
articles.text:
How to turn on Developer Mode on your Chromebook
It's easy, but it's also a little risky.
Chromebooks have earned their reputation as affordable, secure and simple machines over the years. Most owners never venture beyond the Play Store, downloading apps and calling it a day. But much like Android power users, Chromebook owners can take things one step further and unlock a completely different experience by turning on Developer Mode.
Developer Mode strips away many of ChromeOS' built-in protections and gives you full control over the system, which may or may not be a good idea depending on your technical knowledge. Still, you get root access, kernel modifications and the ability to install software that was never on the Play Store. It's a powerful tool, so it's not something you should use without understanding what you're getting into.
So what exactly does Developer Mode do? When does it actually make sense to use it? How do you enable this feature? We'll dig through everything and discuss what changes once Developer Mode is on and whether it's something you need as you use your Chromebook as your everyday computer.
What is Developer Mode on a Chromebook?
Developer Mode is a system setting that gives you more control over how your device operates, relaxing ChromeOS' "verified boot" protections. Normally, ChromeOS runs on a locked-down system. It double-checks itself on every boot, reverting automatically if something looks tampered with and sandboxing every app and webpage so problems can't spread. Developer Mode tears down most of those protections.
As with most systems, once Developer Mode is enabled, you gain full system access. That means you can change the ChromeOS kernel and core files. The trade-off is security. With Verified Boot relaxed, your Chromebook no longer has some of its default defenses against malicious tampering. Lest you forget you made this move, there'll be a visual reminder in the form of a warning screen on startup that reads OS Verification is OFF or You are in Developer Mode. The warning times out after 30 seconds with a warning beep, so there's no way to say you didn't know. It's not a sign of danger, but it's a signal that your system is running without a safety net.
When would you actually need Developer Mode?
Let's be honest here: Developer Mode isn't something the average Chromebook owner needs to think about. Most day-to-day tasks like shooting emails, browsing, streaming, editing documents and so on work just fine within the safety brackets provided by stock ChromeOS.
That said, there are situations when enabling Developer Mode is needed. For instance, while modern ChromeOS includes built-in support for running Linux apps in a secure sandbox, deeper system-level modifications still require Developer Mode. You'll need it if you want full root shell access to the OS, need to load custom Linux kernels or plan to run alternative operating systems. Developer Mode is also required for advanced system tweaks like firmware modifications and boot flag changes.
Also, if you want to quickly double-click and install APK files directly through the native ChromeOS Files app without touching the command line, Developer Mode is required. It's worth noting that ChromeOS now allows you to sideload APKs securely without Developer Mode by enabling Android Debug Bridge inside the official Linux environment. If that's the reason you're looking into Developer Mode, you might want to try this out first.
Of course, Developer Mode is also going to be a feature that actual developers building or debugging apps for ChromeOS might use. If none of these apply to you, there's a strong chance you should leave your Chromebook alone. Note that school- or work-managed Chromebooks usually have Developer Mode blocked by the administrator.
How to turn on Developer Mode
If you still want to turn on Developer Mode, then you need to follow a few steps. One important thing to know is that switching between Normal and Developer Mode wipes all local user data.
- Let's boot the system into Recovery Mode. Press and hold Esc + Refresh + Power simultaneously to do this on a standard Chromebook laptop.
- From the Recovery screen, press Ctrl + D and confirm the prompt that pops up asking whether you want to turn OS Verification off. The system will then reboot.
- Next, you'll see one of two notifications: "You are in Developer Mode" or "OS Verification is OFF" (the exact wording can vary by device). Press Ctrl + D to start the transition right away, or just wait 30 seconds for the beep and it will begin on its own. This is when the local data gets wiped. The process can take up to 15 minutes, so do not interrupt it.
Developer Mode transforms a Chromebook from a simplified, locked-down device into a system that's a lot easier to customize. The cost, however, is your device's security — one of the things that make ChromeOS appealing in the first place, especially for people who were hoping to get an affordable Chromebook to use as their daily driver. For developers or Linux enthusiasts, however, it's a genuinely useful tool. If you decide to enable it, back up your files first, keep your device plugged in and follow the steps carefully.

articles.title: Google, JPMorgan and two governments fixed the same MCP flaw
articles.text:
Security teams at Google, JPMorgan Chase, Weaviate, France’s interministerial digital directorate (DINUM) and the city government of Tangerang in Indonesia have each fixed the same type of flaw in their Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin reported all five, he wrote in an update published this month.
MCP is the standard AI agents use to call tools and data sources. The flaw is server-side request forgery (SSRF). An MCP server takes a URL, path or endpoint from an agent and builds an outbound request from it, without checking where the address actually resolves. That lets whoever steers the agent decide what the server talks to, including internal systems.
In May, Mohiuddin argued that the problem was structural. If it was, he predicted, teams that share no code or owner would all produce it.
“Watching the same mistake come back from a hyperscaler, a bank, and a national government, one report at a time, is the moment the May argument stopped being a guess,” Mohiuddin wrote.
Five fixes
Google’s MCP Toolbox for Databases had an HTTP client with no restrictive redirect policy and no check on target IP addresses, according to the GitHub advisory. A crafted path parameter could send its requests to internal or external endpoints. The flaw, CVE-2026-14540, carries a high rating of 8.0 and affects versions 0.3.0 to 1.4.0. Google’s fix adds a guard against DNS rebinding and lists of allowed and blocked IP ranges, and credits Mohiuddin.
JPMorgan’s open-source repository includes a documentation-search MCP server with two tools that fetch content. One checked domains against an allowlist. Its sibling fetched any URL the caller supplied, Mohiuddin wrote. JPMorgan forked the component from an AWS project that never fetched the caller’s URL at all. JPMorgan’s Responsible Disclosure team confirmed the finding and deployed a fix, he wrote. The finding is medium severity, he wrote.
Weaviate restricted its Google module’s endpoint settings to Google API hosts, he wrote. DINUM’s official MCP server for France’s open-data platform fetched URLs supplied by data producers, which could point at internal or cloud metadata addresses. Its fix, titled “harden SSRF on external APIs”, opens with “Reported by Syed Anas Mohiuddin”.
In Tangerang’s Wazuh MCP server, a tool advertised SSRF protection but only rejected literal IP addresses, according to a high-severity advisory published on 3 September. It never resolved hostnames.
Rapid7 fixed a different bug he found, CVE-2026-97228, in its Bulk Export MCP server. The bug allowed GraphQL injection within the operator’s own access, and Rapid7 rates it low, at 2.7, its database entry says.
Still open
On 2 September, Mohiuddin privately reported issues in five MCP servers under the US General Services Administration’s Technology Transformation Services. They include servers for Veterans Affairs benefits claims, CMS Blue Button, regulations.gov, USASpending and CDC PLACES. All five are still in triage and not fixed, he wrote.
In the Veterans Affairs case, the server logs full error responses from the benefits API without redaction, according to Mohiuddin. Those can contain a veteran’s name, Social Security number, date of birth and address. He is withholding code-level detail until maintainers patch the servers. His report on Japan’s Digital Agency grants server, which had no authentication, also remains open.
‘Protocol pivoting’
Mohiuddin calls the wider attack class “protocol pivoting”. An attacker plants text in content an MCP tool returns, shaped like a task for Google’s A2A protocol. An orchestrating agent passes it to a subagent, which runs it because it trusts the orchestrator.
“Every piece in that chain did exactly what it was designed to do, which is what makes this so tricky to catch,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, told Ars Technica.
Markus Vervier of X41 D-Sec told Ars that the technique is a form of indirect prompt injection. Mohiuddin will present the findings at MCPCon North America in San Jose on 23 October.
