articles.title: HackerRank's AI interviewer offers a glimpse into what job interviews could become | TechCrunch
articles.text:
What happens when AI moves from helping job candidates to evaluating them? HackerRank, a platform used by companies to assess and hire developers, is offering a glimpse at what that future of job interviews could look like with Chakra, an AI agent that conducts interviews, observes candidates as they work, and evaluates not just their answers but also how they got there.
After around six months in beta, HackerRank is making Chakra generally available to its customers on Monday. The startup says the AI interviewer has already conducted more than 500,000 interviews during testing, with companies including Snowflake, Snorkel, and Capgemini among those that tried it, while HackerRank also tested the product internally.
AI has been a staple in job interviews for some time, with companies using voice agents and other automated tools to screen candidates and make the hiring process more efficient. Job seekers, meanwhile, have increasingly gained their own AI tools to help them navigate interviews, sometimes without employers knowing.
With Chakra, HackerRank is betting AI can change not only how interviews are conducted, but also what employers can measure. Beyond whether someone arrives at the right answer, the startup wants to assess harder-to-capture signals such as critical thinking and judgment, as well as what it calls “AI fluency” — how well a candidate frames a problem for AI, judges its output, and steers it toward a solution.
“The previous modality of evaluation was evaluating the output,” HackerRank co-founder and CEO Vivek Ravisankar said in an interview. “Now, because of AI, anybody can produce an artifact.” The question for employers, he said, becomes whether they can understand the thinking and judgment that went into producing it.
In practice, a Chakra interview is designed to look more like doing the job than taking a traditional coding test. A candidate gets a task involving a real-world code repository, and they work through it in a canvas that includes an AI assistant. As the candidate works, Chakra can use the context of what they are doing to ask follow-up questions, such as why they chose one approach over another, or how their solution would change if a new constraint were introduced.
Ravisankar told TechCrunch that Chakra is changing the basic structure of the hiring process itself. What previously involved three separate rounds, comprising a recruiter screen, take-home assessment, and follow-up interview with an engineer, is now combined into a single Chakra interview, he said.
Giving candidates access to AI during an interview might seem to make it easier to cheat. However, HackerRank says it found the opposite. Suspicious-activity flags, Ravisankar said, were 70% to 80% lower in Chakra interviews than in comparable traditional HackerRank assessments, though the rate varied depending on factors such as geography and seniority.
Ravisankar told TechCrunch that giving candidates access to AI reduces the incentive to secretly use outside tools that can feed them answers during an interview.
Launched at TechCrunch Disrupt in 2012, HackerRank built its business around coding challenges, eventually helping companies assess and hire developers based on their technical skills. The Y Combinator-backed startup now has more than 3,000 business customers, including Amazon, Nvidia, Clay, and Replit, and a community of over 30 million developers worldwide.
Chakra represents a bet against the kind of technical assessment business HackerRank spent years building. Its traditional product largely tested whether developers could solve coding problems correctly. Nonetheless, Ravisankar believes AI has made HackerRank’s earlier model less useful to measure engineering ability.
Ravisankar compared the transition internally to Apple moving from the iPod to the iPhone, as the old product still has value, but the new one represents where the startup believes the market is headed. “Chakra is going to be the headline,” he said. “It’s going to be the way that we’re going to move forward.”
However, giving AI a deeper role in evaluating candidates raises a different set of questions, particularly around how much of a hiring decision companies should delegate to an algorithm. Ravisankar told TechCrunch that Chakra is designed to score candidates rather than make the final hiring decision, which remains with humans.
AI, he said, can handle more structured parts of an interview by consistently applying criteria set by an employer, while human interviewers can spend more time determining whether they actually want to work with a candidate and answering questions about the company, team, and role.
“AI is way less biased than humans, if you tune it properly,” Ravisankar said, arguing that an AI system can be instructed to follow the same rubric for every candidate rather than being influenced by factors such as a candidate’s background or education.
Applying the same criteria consistently, however, does not necessarily make an AI system free of bias. Automated hiring tools can inherit or amplify biases from the data, models, and criteria used to build them, prompting regulators to scrutinize their use in employment decisions.
The use of AI in hiring is already drawing regulatory scrutiny. New York City, for instance, requires employers using certain automated employment decision tools to subject them to an independent bias audit and provide notice to candidates before using them. Ravisankar acknowledged that hiring is a regulated area and said complying with such requirements is part of what HackerRank has had to build for.

articles.title: Ngân hàng số bước vào cuộc đua hiệu quả và giá trị
articles.text:
Theo ông Ravi Kittane, chuyên gia tư vấn cấp cao ngành dịch vụ tài chính tại EY, ngân hàng ngày nay không còn chỉ là nơi gửi tiền hay bán sản phẩm tín dụng có sẵn. Khách hàng muốn mọi dịch vụ diễn ra tức thì, đúng vào lúc họ cần.
Chuyên gia EY lấy ví dụ Starling Bank ở Anh. Ngân hàng số này tập trung vào doanh nghiệp nhỏ, tích hợp công cụ tính thuế và phần mềm kế toán ngay trong ứng dụng. Nhờ đó, Starling giành 9,4% thị phần và kéo chi phí phục vụ mỗi khách hàng xuống 42,4 bảng Anh.
Tại Việt Nam, Ngân hàng số Cake by VPBank đi theo hướng tương tự nhưng phục vụ nhiều nhóm khách hàng hơn. Dịch vụ tài chính của Cake được đưa thẳng vào các ứng dụng gọi xe, mua sắm của đối tác. Từ đó, một tài xế công nghệ hay người làm nghề tự do có thể được duyệt khoản vay nhỏ chỉ sau vài thao tác trên điện thoại.
Tập khách hàng cũng mở rộng dần. Từ người trẻ mới bắt đầu quản lý chi tiêu, đến người có thu nhập ổn định cần tiết kiệm, đầu tư và người có nhu cầu nhận tiền từ nước ngoài…
Số lượng người dùng không còn là tất cả
Mở tài khoản trong vài phút, không cần ra quầy. Đó là lời hứa đã giúp ngân hàng số tăng trưởng nhanh trong những năm qua. Năm 2021, ngân hàng số Cake đạt 1 triệu khách hàng chỉ sau 11 tháng. Đến nay, con số đã lên gần 8 triệu.
Nhưng quy mô lớn chưa phải là tất cả. Theo bảng xếp hạng 100 ngân hàng số hàng đầu thế giới 2026 của TABInsights (The Asian Banker), gần 40% ngân hàng trong nhóm dẫn đầu này vẫn chưa có lợi nhuận cả năm. Cuộc đua giờ đây được đo bằng hiệu quả, không chỉ bằng số người dùng.
Ông Nguyễn Hữu Quang, CEO Ngân hàng số Cake, cũng không xem con số khách hàng là cột mốc quan trọng nhất. "Nếu phải chọn một giai đoạn đáng nhớ nhất, tôi nghĩ không phải là lúc Cake đạt một con số khách hàng cụ thể, hay nhận một giải thưởng nào đó, mà là thời điểm chúng tôi nhận ra mô hình đã thực sự vận hành được ở quy mô lớn và có thể tạo ra một mô hình kinh doanh bền vững", ông chia sẻ.
Thời điểm quý III/2024, chỉ sau 3,5 năm hoạt động, Cake đạt điểm hòa vốn EBITDA.
Nhiều giá trị hơn trên mỗi khách hàng
Một chỉ số cho thấy rõ sự thay đổi này là ARPU, tức doanh thu trung bình ngân hàng tạo ra từ mỗi khách hàng. Với Cake, ARPU tăng từ 5 USD năm 2023 lên 25 USD năm 2025 và dự kiến đạt 44 USD trong năm 2026.
Con số này tăng khi khách hàng dùng nhiều dịch vụ hơn trong cùng một ứng dụng: thanh toán, tiết kiệm, thẻ, vay, đầu tư… Hệ sinh thái đối tác đa dạng trong bán lẻ, viễn thông, vận tải… giúp Cake có mặt ở nhiều điểm chạm hàng ngày của người dùng.
"Thành công không còn chỉ được đo bằng việc có thêm bao nhiêu người dùng, mà bằng việc mỗi khách hàng có thể tìm thấy ngày càng nhiều giá trị trong hệ sinh thái của Cake. Khi đó, tăng trưởng không chỉ đến từ việc mở rộng quy mô mà còn từ chiều sâu của mối quan hệ với khách hàng", ông Quang nói.
Hướng đi này nhận được ghi nhận quốc tế. Năm 2026, Euromoney trao cho Cake giải "Ngân hàng số tốt nhất Việt Nam" ở hạng mục Group Level Banking. Đây là hạng mục đo lường ngân hàng số và ngân hàng thương mại truyền thống trên cùng một hệ quy chiếu, với các tiêu chí về hiệu quả vận hành, khả năng sinh lời và năng lực thích ứng.
Có thể thấy, những tiêu chí này cũng gần với các thước đo về an toàn và phát triển bền vững mà ngành ngân hàng hướng tới.
Phía sau kết quả đó là đội ngũ. Cake được HR Asia vinh danh "Nơi làm việc tốt nhất châu Á", với môi trường nơi nhân sự được trao quyền để thử nghiệm và sáng tạo.
Theo CEO Cake, chặng đường tiếp theo không còn là chứng minh mô hình ngân hàng số có khả thi hay không. Mục tiêu là phục vụ nhiều khách hàng hơn và tạo ra nhiều giá trị hơn trên mỗi mối quan hệ với khách hàng.
Thu Loan

articles.title: Gemini Call for Me might tell your mom you’re running late
articles.text:
Google may be expanding its “Call for Me” AI feature beyond business calls so you can use it to send messages to friends and family. Android Authority reports finding a “Gemini Calling” introductory screen in an APK teardown with examples that include “Call Mom and tell her I will be 15 minutes late” and “Call John and ask if he is coming for dinner.”
Gemini Call for Me might tell your mom you’re running late
A rumored Android update would automate personal phone calls with Gemini AI.
Based on those examples, even with this expansion, Gemini would likely be limited to basic, text message-like calls. While Google’s AI might not automate an entire catch-up phone call with your relatives, it could deliver quick messages to people who prefer a phone call, miss texts often, or even still have a landline phone.
Android Authority also says it found “granular permissions” for Gemini actions in individual apps, including what appear to be settings for phone call permissions. These settings would allow users to pick and choose which app capabilities they want to allow Gemini to access, potentially giving users an option to opt out of receiving incoming automated calls from Gemini. However, as Android Authority notes, it’s also possible Google might not publicly release this expansion or the granular Gemini app settings.

articles.title: OpenAI launches visual ads that appear alongside image generation results | TechCrunch
articles.text:
ChatGPT is getting more ads. Specifically, OpenAI is adding visual display ads to its ad product line-up so that ads will appear alongside images that users ask ChatGPT to generate. In addition, the company is expanding its ad measurement tools and partnerships, and developing new ways to determine brand suitability.
The new ads will begin to appear later this month in the U.S. only for now, and will feature products and services from an initial test group of advertisers. The ads will also be clearly labeled and won’t influence the answers ChatGPT provides, the company notes.
The move follows the launch of Meta’s Muse, an agentic AI app which is free to everyone and a growing competitor for leading AI chatbots, like ChatGPT.
OpenAI introduced ads earlier this year to support its free and low-cost subscription tiers, and expanded them to India in August.
Now, the plan is to woo online advertisers who want to appeal to their potential customers by using more visual imagery to tell their stories. Eventually, those ads will allow them to target ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion weekly users, once they roll out globally.
However, integrating such ads could also prove disruptive to the user experience. But perhaps that’s partly the point, as the ads could push more casual users to pay for a subscription in order to avoid them.
Alongside the display ads, OpenAI said it is expanding its measurement tools and partner ecosystem, which now includes click attribution solutions, AppsFlyer, Triple Whale, Adjust, DV Rockerbox, Northbeam, Branch, Singular, Kochava, Airbridge, and Tenjin, as well as full-funnel, advanced measurement partners Fospha, Measured, and INCRMNTAL.
OpenAI has also partnered with Haus, Measured, and WorkMagic to help advertisers explore “geo-based” experiments around ads.
The company said it’s working on developing brand suitability evaluation pilots with help from DoubleVerify (DV) and Integral Ad Science (IAS), which will help advertisers better understand the ChatGPT ads environment.
Combined, the moves see OpenAI working to make ChatGPT a viable ad-supported business for those on free and low-cost plans.

articles.title: OpenAI is testing more ads in ChatGPT - Engadget
articles.text:
OpenAI is testing more ads in ChatGPT
Visual ads will appear first in image generation.
OpenAI is bringing new, more visual ads to ChatGPT. In a blog published Monday, the company said it would begin, starting later this month, to test a new ad format inside of its chatbot. ChatGPT users in the US will be the first to see the new advertisements. They will appear when you go to generate an image using ChatGPT Images. "Ads will be clearly labeled, and remain separate from the image being created," explains OpenAI. "As with our other ad formats, advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides."
OpenAI first began displaying ads inside of ChatGPT at the start of the year. Those ads appear in a sponsored section beneath the chatbot's outputs, with the sponsor's name, logo and a link to its website displayed. By adding visuals to the mix, OpenAI says its ads will help people better imagine how the products and services it recommends "could fit into their lives." If you're a ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscriber, you won't see any ads appear in your chats. Enterprise customers also won't see ads appear in their conversations. OpenAI is testing visual ads with a select group of initial advertisers, and says it plans to experiment with additional formats in the future.
As in the past, OpenAI says it has implemented safeguards to ensure ads are only displayed alongside topics where it would be "appropriate" to advertise something. For instance, you won't see ChatGPT generate ads when you're talking to the chatbot about sensitive topics, such as your personal health or mental wellbeing.

articles.title: ‘You are never truly anonymous’: Anthropic flags Claude chat to police
articles.text:
Sheriff’s deputies have arrested a woman in Florida after Anthropic reported her Claude conversation to law enforcement. In the chat she allegedly said she would “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff’s Office. WINK News first reported the arrest on 30 September.
According to the arrest report, she wrote the statement on 26 September. In a message the following day, she said she had got a new gun.
Anthropic’s platform monitors for key phrases and potentially threatening content, investigators wrote in the report. Because of their severity, the statements went to a human review team. That team reported them to law enforcement.
‘Never truly anonymous’
Deputies detained the woman at her home without incident. An intelligence detective from the sheriff’s office then took over the case. She later said she uses AI like a “diary”, Sheriff Carmine Marceno told WINK News.
“Artificial intelligence is a powerful tool, and like any technology, it can be misused. When someone uses AI to make or facilitate a threat, we have to take that threat seriously. Users need to understand that you are never truly anonymous,” Marceno said in a statement.
Court records list a felony charge filed on 30 September under Florida Statute 836.10, Tom’s Hardware reported. The statute covers written or electronic threats of a mass shooting or act of terrorism. The court appointed a public defender, and her arraignment is set for 2 November.
Anthropic has not commented publicly on the case, according to Tom’s Hardware.
What Anthropic’s policies say
Anthropic’s privacy policy has been in force since 10 September. It says Anthropic may share personal data with law enforcement where it believes in good faith that disclosure is “reasonably necessary” to “prevent serious harm to any person or to property”.
Its policy on government requests says it discloses user information only under valid legal process. The exception is an emergency that “may result in imminent physical harm or death”.
Earlier cases
Tom’s Hardware counts at least two earlier Claude conversations that reached police since August, citing regional news reports. In San Antonio, a 22-year-old man asked “an Anthropic AI chat” on 11 August about shooting at a nearby elementary school. Police, alerted by the FBI, arrested him on a felony terroristic threat charge.
On 14 August in San Francisco, a user threatened Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei in a Claude chat. He said he had bought an AR-15. Anthropic notified police, who did not arrest or charge him.
OpenAI has also reported ChatGPT users. In March, a Florida man wrote to ChatGPT about killing his ex-girlfriend, and OpenAI reported him to the FBI, the Palm Beach Post reported. He pleaded guilty in August to charges including written threats to kill, under the same statute, and was sentenced to eight years’ probation.
Earlier this year, Sam Altman apologised after OpenAI did not alert police about the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s account. Florida’s attorney general, who sued OpenAI in June, is now seeking a court order against the company.

articles.title: Mỏ sắt 16 triệu tấn cách 2km, nhà máy vẫn phải mua quặng từ xa: Gỡ nút thắt sau 15 năm
articles.text:
XEM VIDEO:
Mỗi năm tốn 200 tỷ chở quặng, nhà máy cách mỏ sắt 16 triệu tấn chỉ 2km
Ngày 2/10, máy móc bắt đầu bóc lớp đất hữu cơ trên phần mặt bằng vừa được bàn giao tại khu Bắc mỏ sắt Nà Rụa, Cao Bằng. Đây là bước chuẩn bị khai trường cho vùng quặng hơn 16 triệu tấn, nằm cách Khu liên hợp Gang thép Cao Bằng khoảng 2km nhưng nhiều năm chưa thể khai thác.
Trong thời gian chờ nguồn quặng này, những chuyến xe từ Lào Cai, Thái Nguyên, Tuyên Quang vẫn đưa nguyên liệu về nhà máy tại phường Tân Giang. Có nguồn quặng phải vượt hơn 600km mới tới nơi.
Trong khi đó, khu Bắc mỏ sắt Nà Rụa với hơn 16 triệu tấn quặng nằm cách khu liên hợp chỉ khoảng 2km vẫn chưa thể khai thác.
Từ năm 2024, khi nguồn quặng tại khu Nam Nà Rụa cạn, Công ty CP Gang thép Cao Bằng phải mua toàn bộ quặng từ bên ngoài.
Ông Nguyễn Hoài Nam, Phó Giám đốc công ty, cho biết chi phí vận chuyển bình quân khoảng 300.000 đồng/tấn, có thời điểm lên tới 600.000 đồng/tấn. Mỗi năm, riêng tiền vận tải quặng của doanh nghiệp vào khoảng 200 tỷ đồng.
Nghịch lý ấy kéo dài cùng với những vướng mắc giải phóng mặt bằng tại khu Bắc. Theo lãnh đạo phường Tân Giang, quá trình này kéo dài khoảng 15 năm, liên quan đến hàng trăm hộ dân, nhiều phần mộ và các hồ sơ đất đai có nguồn gốc, hiện trạng sử dụng khác nhau.
Riêng phạm vi khoảng 21ha giai đoạn 1, ban đầu xác định có 421 hộ và 347 ngôi mộ. Sau khi rà soát nguồn gốc đất, quan hệ thừa kế, tách đối tượng và các trường hợp phát sinh, số lượng tăng lên 443 hộ và 364 ngôi mộ.
Đến ngày 24/8/2026, mới có 94 hộ bàn giao hơn 21.300m² mặt bằng.
Để mở khai trường, vấn đề không chỉ là thu hồi đủ diện tích. Từng hồ sơ bồi thường, hỗ trợ, đất ở, tái định cư và di chuyển mồ mả cần được giải quyết.
Rời nơi đã gắn bó hơn 40 năm
Gia đình anh Nguyễn Bằng Giang là một trong những hộ phải di chuyển khỏi vùng quặng khu Bắc Nà Rụa. Năm 1982, khi quanh quả đồi gần như chưa có nhà, bố anh Giang, một người làm địa chất, chọn nơi này dựng nhà và làm trang trại. Gia đình có khoảng 120m² đất ở, 1.500m² đất nông nghiệp, với căn nhà rộng khoảng 90m².
Khoảng năm 2020, anh Giang từng tính cải tạo khu đất thành nhà vườn, làm homestay. Kế hoạch dừng lại khi gia đình phải chuẩn bị bàn giao mặt bằng.
“Ở đây mình gắn bó, sinh ra lớn lên. Mình không muốn bán. Khi phải chuyển đi thì ai cũng tâm tư, buồn chứ”, anh nói.
Theo anh Giang, trước đây gia đình còn nhiều thắc mắc về phương án bồi thường và hỗ trợ đối với đất nông nghiệp. Đến năm 2026, các cuộc đối thoại diễn ra thường xuyên hơn, từng vấn đề được trả lời cụ thể.
“Trả lời đi thẳng, chính xác vào từng câu hỏi”, anh nhận xét.
Sau khi kiến nghị về khoản hỗ trợ chuyển đổi nghề đối với đất nông nghiệp được xem xét lại, gia đình đồng ý phương án và bắt đầu di chuyển.
Gia đình ba thế hệ của anh được bố trí hai lô tái định cư liền kề tại phường Thục Phán, cách nhà cũ khoảng 5km. Hai lô đất cạnh nhau giúp các thành viên có thể tiếp tục sống gần nhau, nhất là khi mẹ anh đã cao tuổi.
Tuy nhiên, nơi ở mới vẫn đang trong quá trình xây dựng. Đầu tháng 10, hệ thống giao thông kết nối và một trường học trong khu vực đang được triển khai.
Câu chuyện của gia đình anh Giang cho thấy, phía sau mỗi phần diện tích bàn giao là phương án bồi thường, sinh kế và chỗ ở sau di dời. Những vấn đề này cần được giải quyết cụ thể để người dân có thể chuyển đi.
Từ 94 lên 434 hộ bàn giao mặt bằng
Trong tháng 8/2026, khu Bắc Nà Rụa được đặt thời hạn mới về giải phóng mặt bằng.
Tại cuộc làm việc giữa lãnh đạo tỉnh Cao Bằng và Tập đoàn Công nghiệp Than - Khoáng sản Việt Nam (TKV) ngày 18/8, mục tiêu được xác định là đến ngày 30/9 cơ bản hoàn thành giải phóng khoảng 21ha trung tâm khai trường.
Trước đó, tại buổi làm việc với TKV ngày 29/7, Tổng Bí thư Tô Lâm yêu cầu tập đoàn tập trung vào lĩnh vực cốt lõi, khai thác và sử dụng tài nguyên tiết kiệm, hiệu quả, đẩy mạnh chế biến sâu.
Ngày 29/8, tỉnh thành lập tổ công tác do ông Lương Tuấn Hùng, Phó Chủ tịch Thường trực UBND tỉnh, làm tổ trưởng để xử lý các vướng mắc tại khu Bắc.
Theo ông Hùng, công việc được phân rõ cơ quan, người phụ trách và thời hạn; cán bộ chuyên môn được tăng cường xuống cơ sở. Những nội dung vượt thẩm quyền được báo cáo Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh kèm phương án xử lý.
Tại phường Tân Giang, cuộc giao ban hằng ngày bắt đầu lúc 7h15. Danh sách được cập nhật đến từng hộ, từng phần mộ và từng hồ sơ: trường hợp nào chưa nhận tiền, còn vướng nguồn gốc đất, cần chỗ tạm cư hoặc chưa thống nhất thời gian di chuyển mộ.
Bốn tổ công tác phụ trách các khâu theo dõi tiến độ; đối thoại với người dân; xử lý hồ sơ bồi thường, chi trả và tái định cư; chuẩn bị chỗ tạm cư, nhân lực, phương tiện hỗ trợ di chuyển.
Một nhóm Zalo chung được lập để tiếp nhận câu hỏi, phản ánh và đơn thư của các hộ. Nội dung được chuyển tới bộ phận phụ trách và phản hồi trên cùng kênh.
Ông Nguyễn Minh Tuệ, Phó Chủ tịch UBND phường Tân Giang, gọi cách làm này là “5 bám”: bám hộ, bám hồ sơ, bám việc, bám tiến độ, bám kết quả.
Trong 37 ngày, phường và các lực lượng liên quan tổ chức hơn 150 cuộc tuyên truyền, vận động, đối thoại; làm việc và tiếp nhận ý kiến của trên 300 trường hợp.
Đến hết ngày 30/9, có 434/443 hộ bàn giao mặt bằng, tăng 340 hộ so với ngày 24/8. Diện tích bàn giao đạt 207.389m²; 354/364 ngôi mộ đã được di chuyển.
Trong toàn dự án, 227 lô tái định cư đã được tổ chức bốc thăm; 23 hộ có nhu cầu tạm cư được bố trí nơi ở.
Dù phần lớn diện tích đã được bàn giao, công việc giải phóng mặt bằng chưa kết thúc. Tính đến hết tháng 9, còn 9 hộ chưa bàn giao và 10 ngôi mộ chưa di chuyển.
Bổ sung dây chuyền cán thép, tránh 'hai lần lãng phí'
Phần mặt bằng vừa được bàn giao giúp doanh nghiệp bắt đầu chuẩn bị khai trường, nhưng chưa thể lập tức thay thế nguồn quặng mua ngoài.
Theo ông Nguyễn Hoài Nam, sau bước bóc lớp đất hữu cơ, công ty dự kiến từ ngày 5/10 triển khai bóc đất khai trường. Kế hoạch năm 2026 là bóc khoảng 600.000m³ đất; năm 2027 khoảng 2,2 triệu m³.
Doanh nghiệp dự kiến khai thác khoảng 70.000 tấn quặng trong năm 2027, tăng lên 120.000 tấn năm 2028 và hướng tới công suất 350.000 tấn/năm từ năm 2029.
Như vậy, việc tháo gỡ mặt bằng mới mở đường cho giai đoạn chuẩn bị và khai thác. Khả năng giảm chi phí vận tải còn phụ thuộc vào tiến độ đưa quặng khu Bắc vào sản xuất và sản lượng thực tế.
Cùng với kế hoạch khai thác mỏ, Công ty CP Gang thép Cao Bằng đang triển khai dây chuyền cán thép công suất khoảng 70.000 tấn/năm.
Hiện phôi thép sau khi ra lò phải chờ nguội để vận chuyển đi nơi khác cán, rồi được nung nóng trở lại trước khi đưa qua dây chuyền. Chủ tịch UBND tỉnh Cao Bằng Lê Hải Hòa gọi đây là tình trạng “hai lần lãng phí”. Do đó, việc bổ sung công đoạn cán tại khu liên hợp được kỳ vọng giảm khâu vận chuyển và nung lại phôi.
Mục tiêu đặt ra là đưa dây chuyền vào vận hành trong quý I/2027. Theo kế hoạch, dây chuyền cần khoảng 130 lao động, với thu nhập bình quân dự kiến 12 triệu đồng/người/tháng.
Nếu các hạng mục được triển khai đúng tiến độ, quặng Nà Rụa sẽ được đưa vào chuỗi khai thác, luyện gang, sản xuất phôi và cán thép tại Cao Bằng.
Sau khoảng 15 năm kéo dài, những chiếc máy bóc đất đầu tiên đánh dấu bước chuyển của khu Bắc Nà Rụa. Nhưng từ mặt bằng đã bàn giao đến nguồn quặng phục vụ nhà máy vẫn còn khoảng cách: hoàn tất di dời, chuẩn bị khai trường và thực hiện kế hoạch khai thác trong những năm tới.

articles.title: Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
articles.text:
It’s a wild time for retro gaming. Thanks to decompilations and recompilations of classic titles, those games are becoming unshackled from their proprietary code and original hardware to be ported to new devices or updated in ways to completely change the original game. Ever imagined skateboarding in Call of Duty? Or playing the original Halo right in your web browser, complete with multiplayer?
Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports
These are unofficial versions of games, so they may sit in a legal gray area. It seems unlikely that Nintendo, for example, is particularly happy about people finding ways to play The Legend of Zelda on non-Nintendo hardware. Many of these projects are also made with the assistance of AI, which, for some people, is a non-starter given ethical or environmental concerns surrounding the technology.
Below, you’ll find our coverage of gaming decomps, recomps, and all the other ways gamers are reverse-engineering games to go previously unimaginable places.
- Here’s a video of Half-Life: Alyx running natively on a Vision Pro. Take a look. It was “made possible” thanks in part to Valve’s ARM port of the game it made for the Steam Frame and with some help from Claude.
- Just think: You could be playing Halo in a web browser right now. The video game decompilation movement has done it again. Not only do we have 128 player Halo across Windows, Linux, and Android , you can also just fire it up in a web browser thanks to OpenHaloCE and immediately start campaign or a huge multiplayer match. It’s not just one dev: lots of people made this happen.
- This unofficial Lego Racers remake runs in your browser with split-screen and online multiplayer. The classic game decompilation movement has produced yet another amazing feat: 1999’s Lego Racers isn’t just back, the excellent Mario-Kart-meets-Lego game is anywhere you want it to be. NavigatorSharp’s fan recreation Step On It works in a web browser on desktop or phone, and you can find builds for Android, Mac, Windows PC and Linux (including the Steam Deck) right here too.
- How an online community took back the Legend of Zelda I don’t have a first memory of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time because It’s been in my life for as long as I can remember. Before I had the coordination to play the game myself, I would watch my older brothers play it for hours on end. When I could finally play through it myself, it felt like flying. I chase that dopamine hit once every year or two by playing through Ocarina of Time, which normally requires dusting off my old GameCube and hoping the disk isn’t too scratched to read. But for the last several months, I haven’t been playing Ocarina of Time on a Nintendo console at all. Instead, I’ve been playing it on something called Ship of Harkinian: an unofficial port of Ocarina of Time for PC that a few short years ago would have been unimaginable. Read Article >

articles.title: Elon Musk’s Exes Are the Most Damning Part of a Massive New Documentary
articles.text:
On Friday morning, Shivon Zilis, a top executive and lieutenant of Elon Musk at his brain chip implant company Neuralink—as well as mother of four of the 14 children he is known to have fathered—took to his social media platform, X, to announce an abrupt shift in their relationship.
“It’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week with no warning, but that’s just how it is sometimes,” Zilis wrote, sharing a screenshot of the X account @BigTechAlert that showed Musk had unfollowed her there. Zilis’ post continued: “I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,” followed by warm praise and best wishes for Musk. “I do hope and pray he and I can be great friends and coparents,” Zilis concluded, leaving some ambiguity as to what exactly changed between them and whether she remains a director of operations and special projects at Neuralink, though it does not appear as if she has left the position.
While this was a strange revelation of a private matter, it seemed hardly out of the ordinary for Musk’s dizzyingly complicated family life. At this point, all four of the women confirmed to have had children with him—Zilis, ex-wife Justine Wilson, Claire Boucher (better known as Grimes), and Ashley St. Clair—have used X to share details of their time with him or push back against his own claims.
Both Wilson and St. Clair participated in filmmaker Alex Gibney’s sprawling new documentary Musk, in theaters nationwide on October 16 and screening at the WIRED World Fair in Miami next month. St. Clair, a former conservative influencer, alleges that she rejected a nondisclosure agreement worth $40 million that would have prevented her from talking about her tumultuous association with Musk. Among an ensemble of tech entrepreneurs, journalists, and former Musk employees, the pair stand out as arguably the most important critical voices in the film, shedding light on Musk’s rise in Silicon Valley as well as his turn toward MAGA extremism during the 2024 election.
At a run time of nearly four hours, Musk sounds like daunting viewing, though once it’s over, you’ll find yourself wondering if it could’ve been a 10-part miniseries. That’s how much ground there is to cover, from the unrealistic ambitions of landing on Mars and the corporate colonization of Texas to the fatal collisions involving “self-driving” Teslas and the annihilation of the US Agency for International Development by the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) at the beginning of Trump’s second term. (WIRED’s reporting is cited in the documentary, which features interviews with global editorial director Katie Drummond and contributing editor Zoë Schiffer.)
Alongside a fast-moving, comprehensive account of Musk’s career as an all-powerful and untouchable oligarch, his former romantic partners provide crucial context about exactly who he is, piecing together a devastating portrait of the type of man to “let go” of a significant other by unfollowing her on social media.
Wilson reflects movingly on the loss of their firstborn to a SIDS-related condition, which is juxtaposed with a Musk post on X in which he wrote that he held their infant son as he died—a comment to which his ex-wife replied, “not that it matters to anyone except me, because it is one of the most sacred and defining moments of my life, but I was the one who was holding him.”
In the film, she also addresses the pain of Musk repeatedly insisting that their transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, was “killed by the woke mind virus,” calling this an unconscionable comment given the actual loss of a child they experienced together. Musk goes on to tell Gibney that right after passing along the message that he would “always love” Wilson, he cut off their daughter’s health insurance and that he has “never tried to repair things” with her.
“He was constantly remarking on the ways he found me lacking,” Wilson says in recounting their marriage. She claims that when she reminded her husband that she was his spouse and not an employee, he told her, “If you were my employee, I would fire you.” Summing up their overall dynamic, she says: “I learned the term gaslighting through my relationship with Elon.”
St. Clair, defiantly outspoken against Musk since revealing in early 2025 that he had fathered a child with her, alleges that her whirlwind affair with the billionaire was a temporary illusion of compatibility that led to a messy and ongoing custody battle. (Musk also covers a custody dispute with Grimes that was eventually settled for undisclosed terms.) St. Clair says in the film that Musk lost interest in her once she was pregnant and claims that he sought to father children with other women. According to The Wall Street Journal, this included cryptocurrency influencer Tiffany Fong, whom he messaged with an offer to give her a child. (Musk did not immediately return a request for comment on this matter. Fong declined to comment publicly on the Journal’s story except to say that she had requested not to be included in the outlet’s reporting.)
“It’s like a Gatling gun of sperm in his DMs,” St. Clair quips. In the film’s interviews, both she and Wilson voice discomfort over their ex’s views on birth rates and ambition to father a “legion” of offspring, with Wilson claiming he regards the mothers of his children as replaceable “breeders.”
Elsewhere in the film, St. Clair covers her allegation that Musk retaliated against her by reducing his financial support for their son, Romulus. And her reluctance to touch on certain issues the filmmakers ask her about seems to serve as something of an answer in its own right. “I’m not at liberty to say,” she responds carefully when asked if she ever witnessed Musk using illegal drugs.
Gibney’s broad account of how Musk wove together a tech empire and his celebrity image through relentless self-mythologizing, then insulated it from government oversight by backing Trump and seizing power within his administration, is an utterly convincing one. But most of the story will be familiar to those who have kept up with Musk headlines for the past decade. What’s truly eye-opening in Musk is the way the women he was once close to talk about what they see as his boundless capacity for cruelty and narcissism.
Is there a world in which Zilis, too, comes forward to share her intimate conversations and correspondence with Musk? That surely depends on whether she has signed any legal documents like those presented to St. Clair. What’s more than evident, however, is that for all his resources, Musk can’t buy the silence of everyone he’s ever known, and if anyone can finally shred his aura of genius inventor-king, it’s the women he’s allowed—however briefly—to share his orbit.

articles.title: Lola Vision Systems is trying to make it easier to run AI models on chips | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The story begins almost 12 years ago, when Tayo Adesanya started a career working with microchips and AI processors. He mainly helped large manufacturers decide which chips to use in their hardware. Those years, he told TechCrunch, gave him early insight into where demand in the AI computing market was headed. “Starting Lola Vision Systems was a bet on where the world was headed and what I was seeing,” he said.
In 2024, he launched Lola Vision Systems, an AI infrastructure company that builds software and chips for running AI models on devices. Its core product is software that translates AI models into instructions a specific chip can run. Adesanya calls this software a “compiler toolchain,” and he says it is a massive bottleneck: Manually setting up an AI model on new hardware can take “roughly 200 hours” just to begin testing. Lola Vision says it has rebuilt that software layer and is also developing its own semiconductor chips, with the goal of automating more of the process. A client provides its code and the AI model it wants to use, whether custom-built or open source, and the software translates both into instructions the client’s chip can execute.
“Speed is only part of it,” Adesanya said. He explained that faster setup gives aerospace and “other mission-critical companies” time to “run more accurate models on their own data, at a lower power.”
“For these customers,” he said, “accuracy and reliability aren’t nice to have. They determine whether a product passes regulatory review and whether it works reliably in the field.”
Lola Vision, based in Washington, D.C., is one of several startups trying to offer an alternative to Nvidia’s technology for running AI on devices. Right now, Adesanya said, many companies start with Nvidia’s Jetson, a line of compact computing modules for running AI on devices, or with open source AI models. Adesanya claimed these “often break or run poorly out of the box, so teams spend days or weeks getting them to run at all, then even more weeks debugging until the models are usable.”
“Even then,” he continued, “power consumption often blows edge computing budgets, or the board can’t deliver enough compute for the medium to large models the product actually needs to run successfully. This leads to the recognition models lagging behind targets or misreading objects.” (Edge computing means running AI directly on a device, such as a camera or drone, rather than in a remote data center. Recognition models are AI systems that identify objects.)
According to the company, a dozen corporate customers have signed letters expressing interest in buying Lola Vision’s chips once they are available, and it already has one signed customer. It has also partnered with SCALE, a microelectronics workforce development program, to work with more semiconductor labs. “To get revenue sooner, we will now license our software on existing hardware,” Adesanya said. (In other words, rather than waiting for its own chips, the company will let customers pay to use its software on chips that already exist.) He added that the company has raised just over $1 million in total funding to date.
Lola Vision was selected for this year’s TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200, a group of 200 startups chosen for the program. “TechCrunch was a favorite when I was a student at Purdue,” he said. After about a year of building the product and signing its first customer, he said, he felt it was time to apply to Startup Battlefield and get the company in front of a wider audience.
As for what he’s most excited about when it comes to the event, it’s “making meaningful connections and learning as much as I can about what’s happening in and around our space,” he said. “And, to be direct, I’m looking forward to investors writing checks.”
To learn more about Lola Vision Systems and dozens of other highly vetted startups that are joining us at TechCrunch Disrupt next week (along with the VCs coming to check them out), join us in San Francisco, October 13-15.

articles.title: Siri can index more of your personal data — here's how to limit it - Engadget
articles.text:
Siri can index more of your personal data — here's how to limit it
If you’re concerned about Apple’s new digital assistant, here’s how you can restrict its access to your data.
With the release of iOS 27, Apple has finally begun rolling out its long delayed redesign of Siri. You'll need to join a waitlist before you can get Siri AI, but once you gain access to the new digital assistant, you're likely to find it's a significant leap over its predecessor. Engadget's Mat Smith found the new Siri much improved when he tested it on the iOS 27 beta, thanks to its ability to deliver smarter, more personalized responses.
However, there is a downside worth mentioning. Apple partnered with Google to train the new large language models that power Siri AI's features. And as with any AI system, the new Siri requires a great deal of data to work at its best, and that data comes from you(r phone).
How does Siri AI access data from your apps?
The reason Siri AI can provide a more personalized experience is thanks to a framework called App Intents that allows Apple Intelligence tools, including Siri, to access data from the apps on your Apple devices. When you enable Siri AI on your iPhone, iPad or Mac, Spotlight and Siri are unified under a single interface. By default, when you ask Siri a question, it will search through your Apple apps, including Notes and Messages, to pull information that might be relevant to your prompt or query. If a developer has chosen to support App Intents, Siri will be able to scan through their apps too.
Siri AI relies on a combination of on-device models and Apple's Private Cloud Compute (PCC) infrastructure, meaning the assistant will sometimes offload your data to a remote server for processing. Apple says it does not store any data sent to its PCC servers after processing a request, and that it can't even see the data. Still, you might feel uncomfortable about sharing data regardless. Thankfully, there are ways you can control what Siri can index.
Restrict Siri AI's access to content inside your apps
As mentioned, Apple has left it up to developers to decide if Siri AI can access the data people generate inside of their apps. That means as long as they allow iOS 27's Spotlight tool to index the contents of their apps, Siri AI can in turn access and surface that information for you as a user. However, you still have control over the process, and can ultimately decide to restrict Siri from accessing your apps. To do so, follow these steps:
- Open the Settings app.
- Scroll down and tap Apps.
- Select the app you want to restrict Siri from accessing.
- Tap Search.
- Toggle off Show Content in Search.
After you disable Show Content in Search in relation to a particular app, Siri won't pull information from that app, even if you ask it to do so directly. For example, if you disable indexing of Messages, and ask Siri to summarize a series of messages from your friend, the digital assistant will tell you it can't find those messages.
In the Apps settings menu, you may have noticed a collection of options grouped under "Apple Intelligence & Siri." For the purposes of this guide, you can leave those alone; they don't have privacy implications. Instead, they primarily control where iOS might suggest an app for you. For instance, if you disable the "Suggest App" option, you won't see that specific app among the "Siri Suggestions" iOS generates when you access your iPhone's search shade. The "Learn from this App" option sounds nefarious, but it merely allows iOS to see how and when you're using your apps so that it can tailor when it surfaces those apps for you.
On-screen awareness
Even after you restrict Siri's ability to search through your apps, you can still get it to help you with situations requiring contextual knowledge on a more ad-hoc basis. A feature called on-screen awareness allows Siri to read the contents of screenshots and images. This can be useful from an accessibility standpoint, or if you want Siri to summarize a lengthy article or message thread. Just note if you snap a screenshot and ask Siri to interpret it, it might be sent to the company's PCC servers.
Ensure you're not sharing Siri recordings with Apple
By default, Apple won't collect or use the data from your interactions with Siri to train future versions of the virtual assistant. But as part of your iPhone's setup process, you might have accidently opted into sharing your Siri recordings and transcripts with the company. Either way, it's worth checking to confirm your Siri data isn't being used for model training.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Privacy & Security.
- Scroll down and select Analytics & Improvements.
- Disable Improve Siri & Dictation if turned on.
Disable Siri AI altogether
One final option worth mentioning is that you can revert to the older version of Siri. This gives you a way to continue using apps like CarPlay with your voice while limiting your privacy exposure. Unintuitively, however, you'll find the option to do this hidden inside the Screen Time section.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Screen Time, followed by Content & Privacy Restrictions.
- Enable Content & Privacy Restrictions.
- Tap Siri.
- Under Allowed Siri Version, select Siri Classic.
Alternatively, you can disable Siri entirely by following the steps below.
- Open the Settings app.
- Tap Siri.
- Scroll down and select Turn off Siri.
If you want to restrict any other part of the Apple Intelligence suite, Apple has helpful support page on the topic.

articles.title: San Diego County sues AppLovin over explicit ads on kids’ devices
articles.text:
San Diego County has sued AppLovin, a mobile advertising technology company. The county alleges that AppLovin bypassed parental controls to serve ads for adult dating services, alcohol, vaping and graphic sexual content in games played by children. The complaint was filed with San Diego Superior Court on Monday, Bloomberg reported.
According to the complaint, AppLovin collected sensitive data from children’s devices even when parental controls and ad-tracking opt-outs were enabled. This included “information precise enough to pinpoint where kids live, where they study and whether they are sleeping”.
Apple and Google offer ways to block ad tech companies from tracking children’s digital activity. The complaint says AppLovin bypassed these settings with fingerprinting. It used the technique to track children for ad targeting without parental consent, the complaint alleges.
AppLovin “disregards child safety tools to harvest children’s sensitive personal information” to “feed it into the company’s artificial intelligence advertising engine”, the complaint says.
What the screenshots show
The suit alleges that AppLovin shows ads depicting sex acts, such as bondage, in apps marked appropriate for kids. One screenshot in the complaint shows an ad for a sexualised AI chatbot app in a physics-based puzzle game. The game was installed on an Android device configured for a six-year-old, with Google’s parental controls enabled. Another screenshot shows ads for cannabis gummies on a device with the same controls.
AppLovin did not immediately respond to Bloomberg’s request for comment.
“AppLovin does not knowingly collect personal information from children or serve Advertisements to children,” its policies for ad buyers say.
The policies, in force since 18 June, prohibit sexually explicit or other adult content, tobacco and nicotine, and illegal drugs. Alcohol ads need AppLovin’s approval. Ads to children, and ads for products generally prohibited for under-18s, are barred. Advertisers are “solely responsible” for determining whether a user qualifies as a child, the policies say.
Earlier fingerprinting claims
In 2025, short sellers Fuzzy Panda and Muddy Waters accused AppLovin of harvesting proprietary identifiers from other platforms in an unauthorised manner. They said it used them to track users across websites and apps. Chief executive Adam Foroughi wrote in a March 2025 blog post that the reports were “littered with inaccuracies”. He denied creating “alternative accurate and persistent identifiers, typically called device fingerprints”.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission probed AppLovin’s data collection, Bloomberg reported in October 2025, citing people familiar with the matter. The SEC was responding to a whistleblower complaint and the short-seller reports, they said. It had not accused AppLovin of wrongdoing. Chief financial officer Matt Stumpf said on an earnings call in August that the agency had closed its investigation without recommending enforcement action.
A new county unit
The San Diego case is one of three filed on Monday by the county’s new Consumer Fairness and Public Protection Unit. Local officials set it up in response to what they describe as dwindling federal enforcement of consumer protections. In July, a judge cleared several US states to try their claim that Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram.
The unit is also suing Roblox, for inadequate protections to stop adults posing as children and contacting young users. Roblox already faces other lawsuits over child safety. In May, two advocacy groups asked the FTC to investigate it. The third suit targets 3D-printing materials firm Polymaker, for marketing certain materials to people assembling illegal, untraceable guns.
The shareholder suit
AppLovin also faces a securities class action in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Stephen Talbot filed it on 16 September. It names the company, Foroughi and Stumpf.
The complaint covers investors who bought or acquired AppLovin securities between 12 February and 5 August 2026. AppLovin told investors it was “constantly improving” its AI models, the complaint says.
“We don’t really see a reason why that’s going to slow down,” the company told investors, according to the complaint.
The suit alleges that the defendants overstated how constantly AppLovin was improving its AI models. It says they overstated the benefits of the “virtuous cycle” and “compounding” value proposition the models offered. It also alleges that the generative AI video creative feature for AppLovin Ads faced significant development delays. These made its release on AppLovin’s timeline unlikely, the suit alleges.
Two falls in the share price
On 13 July, a Bank of America Securities analyst note said that “AppLovin’s eCommerce footprint expanded at a slower pace in June”. Weekly data had “not shown a clear uptick” since AppLovin Ads opened to all e-commerce advertisers on 22 June, the note said. The shares fell $64.13, or 12.65%, from $506.80 to $442.85.
After the market closed on 5 August, AppLovin reported quarterly revenue of $1.92bn, against consensus estimates of $1.94bn. It attributed the miss in part to delays in rolling out the video tool, according to the complaint. The shares fell $82.13 the next day, or 19.66%, from $417.80 to $335.67.
“Our pace of meaningful model improvement was lighter than normal during the quarter,” management said on 5 August, according to the complaint.
Foroughi also said the video tool was “still [a] work in progress”, the complaint says. AppLovin lost more than $44bn of its market capitalisation across the two falls, according to law firm Hagens Berman. The firm has opened an investigation into the claims.
Investors have until 16 November to ask the court to appoint them to lead the case.

articles.title: Astronomers Confirm Discovery of the Youngest Known Exoplanet Ever
articles.text:
How are planets born, and how do they grow? This is an essential question in astronomy, one that researchers try to answer by observing “young planets.” That’s easier said than done. All the planets in our solar system are the same age, 4.6 billion years old. Astronomers therefore need to look elsewhere to find planets that have formed more recently—making exoplanets enticing research grounds.
Still, the vast majority of the approximately 6,000 exoplanets confirmed to date are also billions of years old. That’s not because there aren’t youthful planets out there, but old planets are easier to discover using common techniques such as the transit method, in which astronomers detect the slight dimming of a star’s light as a planet passes in front of it.
Newly formed exoplanets are often buried within disks of gas and dust, the leftover building blocks from a planet's formation, also known as a protoplanetary disk. The difficulty of just locating such a new celestial body is part of what makes the discovery of the exoplanet Elias 2-24b—now the youngest ever confirmed—so exciting.
The research team, led by Andrea Bernardi at Diego Portales University in Chile, identified the exoplanet by focusing on seven protoplanetary disks where there were notable gaps in the dense matter, since it is believed that growing planets carve out such voids. They reanalyzed “coronagraph” data, in which the central star is blocked out, making the dim reflected light from surrounding celestial bodies stand out.
Scientists had known about a gap in the disk surrounding the star Elias 2-24 for nearly a decade. The European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope (yes, that’s its official name) had detected a point of light within this gap, sparking an ongoing debate over whether it was truly a planet. The researchers used data collected in 2018 and 2020 at the W.M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to compare the dot’s positions over the years. They concluded that this bright spot was not an unrelated background star or noise from the equipment, but rather a celestial object gravitationally bound to Elias 2-24—in other words, a planet.
Elias 2-24b is located approximately 450 light-years from Earth. It orbits its star at a distance of approximately 55 astronomical units (one astronomical unit being the average distance between Earth and the sun). Its mass is estimated to be at most 1.9 to 4.0 times that of Jupiter, though researchers believe its volume is likely to be much smaller than our local gas giant. Since its host star is less than 1 million years old, Elias 2-24b is estimated to be similarly young.
Until now, the youngest exoplanets confirmed through direct observation were those orbiting the stars PDS 70 and WISPIT 2, both of which are over 5 million years old. This new discovery breaks those records by a significant margin.
And Elias 2-24b has a few attributes that require reevaluating some planetary formation models. One of the standard theories is known as the “core accretion model,” which posits that giant planets are formed when a solid core grows more massive and attracts surrounding gas. The time required for formation varies depending on the conditions of the calculation, but according to NASA, it should take about 5 million years for a Jupiter-sized planet to form. That’s also given Jupiter’s distance from the sun, approximately 5 astronomical units. For a planet with a much farther removed orbit like Elias 2-24b, accruing this mass should take even longer.
However, Elias 2-24b doesn’t seem to be following these rules. Despite being 55 astronomical units from its host star, it’s already a giant and behaving like a planet after a remarkably short 1 million years. The research team believes this planet was formed through core accretion, which would mean that this model can produce giant planets much faster than previously assumed.
Lucas Siesa, a professor at Diego Portales University and coauthor of the paper, pointed out in a press release, “Elias 2-24 b shows us that even our best planet-formation models are still missing some important processes.”
What can improve these models is finding more young planets, which may soon be more possible than ever. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched by NASA this past August, is equipped with an even more powerful coronagraph than the one the researchers used to locate Elias 2-24b. Astronomers therefore hope to soon detect more young planets as well as other planets obscured by their bright stars.
“This is just the beginning of a new era of discovery,” Siesa said. “It’s incredible that with modern technology, we are actually able to see planet formation in action, and Roman will take planet hunting to the next level.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

articles.title: The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
articles.text:
The Matic is our favorite robot vacuum and robo-mop, and it’s also now the first to escape the FCC’s Roomba ban.
The Matic is the first robovac to get an FCC ban waiver, not that it needs it
Unlike the router companies, Matic is publicly committing to US manufacturing.
Well, sort of — because the Matic wasn’t banned to begin with.
Here’s what’s actually happening: On October 2nd, the FCC added the original Matic, model 4MA0001, and its charging dock model 4DK0008 to its ban waiver list. That allows the FCC to approve these radio products for import, marketing, and sale.
But the Matic doesn’t need a waiver, because its radios were already approved years ago. The FCC’s foreign drone, robot, and router bans only keep future products from getting imported into the United States, not existing ones whose radios have already been approved.
Besides, Matic’s products don’t get FCC approval to begin with — instead, Matic ships them with an off-the-shelf Intel AX210 Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip that gets its own approval from the FCC. (It’s the same kind of Wi-Fi card you’ll find inside a desktop or laptop computer.) Matic also doesn’t need to worry about an import ban specifically, because Matic assembles its robots right here in Mountain View, California.
A waiver could theoretically help if Matic were to build new products outside the United States and try to import them here, except that the FCC hasn’t granted Matic a blanket approval on a brand of robot, like it did with Asus and Netgear’s routers. Instead, it specifically granted a waiver for the Matic models 4MA0001 and 4DK0008, which, again, have already made it through the FCC.
The waiver might not be completely symbolic. The FCC is currently trying to close lots of the loopholes that currently make its ban impotent, is weighing whether to make manufacturers disclose all the components in their gadgets, and is retroactively cracking down on some companies it sees as flaunting the rules. While Matic assembles its robots in the US, it admits it doesn’t yet source 65 percent of its components from US suppliers, the threshold for it to be seen as Made in the US, and perhaps one of those foreign components could trip it up if not for the waiver.
Even so, Matic already gets its “core compute platform” from Nvidia, co-founder and CEO Mehul Nariyawala tells The Verge, and sources other “critical components” from US companies “whenever possible.”
And unlike some of the other companies where the FCC has mysteriously granted a waiver, Matic is committing to more US manufacturing and onshoring.
“Up till 3 months ago, both our R&D offices and production facilities were in the same office in Mountain View, about 24,000 square feet,” Nariyawala tells The Verge. “We’ve turned that entire facility into production facility and moved our office to Menlo Park.”
He says Matic went from shipping 1,500 robots a year ago to 17,000 now, and is trying to find more and more US suppliers so it can use even fewer foreign parts.
“At the moment we might be the only floor cleaning robot built in America,” he says. “That is becoming one of the key value propositions for our product.”

articles.title: Are phone coolers actually worth it? - Engadget
articles.text:
Are phone coolers actually worth it?
Phone coolers aren't snake oil. They're just solving a problem most people don't have.
The short answer is no, at least for most people. That may sound strange in a discussion about phone coolers, but this isn't a clickbait question with an obvious answer hiding at the bottom. Active cooling can help prevent heat from degrading a phone's sustained performance. But most folks simply don't push their phones hard enough, for long enough, for this to become an issue.
Put enough strain on your phone, and heat can become an issue. Like using your MacBook outside, when temperatures get too high, performance may drop while charging can slow. A phone cooler can help with this, though most of us don't need one.
Active phone coolers work, but that's only half the question
The term "phone cooler" covers a broad spectrum of gadgets. Basic models circulate air over the back of the phone, while thermoelectric (Peltier) coolers draw heat away with a cold plate. Passive cooling cases spread heat over a greater area. Then there are so-called "cooling apps," which may lower workloads or alter performance settings but can't magically remove heat from the hardware.
The real question is whether heat is hurting performance. The CPU and GPU produce plenty of heat when they're busy, and when a phone gets too hot, it begins throttling performance to protect itself. You may notice this in a game that performs well at first, but slows down as the phone heats up.
External cooling can make a measurable difference here. Notebookcheck found 3DMark stability scores of 77 percent and 79.2 percent on the ASUS ROG Phone 8 Pro without the AeroActive Cooler X, compared with 92.7 percent and 90.8 percent with the cooler attached. (In this test, higher percentages are better, representing consistent frame rates even as the device heats up.)
So does a phone cooler reduce lag? Yes, if heat is causing it. It won't fix poor Wi-Fi, server lag caused by physical distance or a game your phone simply can't run well.
Most people can solve the problem without buying another gadget
The obvious case where someone would need a phone cooler is long gaming sessions, particularly if performance suffers once the phone has been under heavy load for a while. The same issue can occur with livestreaming, video processing, outdoor summer photography sessions and other sustained workloads.
Another surprising example is excessive phone heating in cars. Navigation, high screen brightness, charging and direct sunlight can pile on the kind of heat an active cooler is meant to combat. Before purchasing one, however, try positioning the phone near an AC vent (assuming the ambient temperature is high enough to do so comfortably).
Mounting the phone where cool air can circulate around it might resolve the issue without another powered accessory on the dashboard. Removing a thick case, taking the phone out of direct sunlight or avoiding demanding tasks during charging can also help.
Gaming while charging deserves some consideration because charging generates extra heat. Definitely avoid wireless charging, as that runs hotter than standard charging with a cable. Some Galaxy phones offer an option to pause USB PD charging when gaming, a feature (on compatible hardware) that can power the device during gameplay without continually charging the battery. This tackles part of the problem before an external cooler enters the picture.
If your phone repeatedly throttles during extended workloads and simple solutions aren't working, a dedicated phone cooler starts to make sense. Otherwise, you're adding weight, fan noise, likely another cable and maybe something that interferes with your grip, all just to make the back of your phone colder.

articles.title: Nokia CEO says data centres would go up twice as fast if supply allowed
articles.text:
Nokia’s chief executive Justin Hotard says the industry would build data centres twice as fast if memory and energy supply allowed, and that demand would hold even without a new frontier model for three years. Bain and a paper presented at the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity both question whether the revenue exists to pay for what is already being built.
Nokia’s chief executive says the industry would build data centres twice as fast if it could. Justin Hotard told CNBC that nothing about the present pace counts as overbuilding. A paper presented in Washington last month puts the eventual bill at $10.3T.
“If we could build 2x faster, our customers could build 2x faster, they probably would,” he said on CNBC’s The Tech Download podcast. That is why he thinks the buildout is still early. Memory chips and energy are the shortages he named.
Hotard ran Intel’s data centre and AI group before Nokia hired him in 2025.
He also said the demand does not depend on new models arriving. “Even if we didn’t have another frontier model released in the next three years, we could probably make tremendous progress just deploying the technology that’s there today,” he said.
Nokia sells the connections rather than the chips, making the equipment that links racks inside a data centre and links data centres to each other. Those sales doubled to EUR 446M in the second quarter, against group sales of EUR 4.82B.
The shares are up about 130% in a year.
The memory shortage he names has already reached European shelves, with DDR5 prices in Germany up 414% in a year and memory taking as much as half the bill of materials on a budget phone.
Not everyone accepts that the demand will be there.
Bain said last week that AI needs $6T a year by 2031 to pay for the data centres now being built, against the $1.2T to $1.8T that today’s products could generate.
Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh’s paper for the Brookings Papers on Economic Activity puts investment at $10.3T between 2025 and 2032, an average of 3.63% of American GDP a year. He writes that it would be larger relative to the economy than the canal, railway, electrification, highway and telecommunications booms.
He also warns that the financing is moving off balance sheets, into joint ventures, private credit and special purpose vehicles.
Europe has no figure of that kind. Nokia is headquartered in Espoo and most of its customers are not.
The EU opened bidding in July for seven AI gigafactories worth EUR 30B, of which about EUR 1B of public money is actually committed, while the fastest-growing part of Nokia sells into somebody else’s buildout.

articles.title: This startup is issuing AI-generated acne prescriptions
articles.text:
People in Utah can now use AI to get a prescription for acne treatment. On Monday, healthcare startup Nolla Health announced that users in the state can scan their faces using its app, allowing its AI system to analyze acne severity and autonomously write a prescription, as reported earlier by Bloomberg.
This startup is issuing AI-generated acne prescriptions
Utah has signed off on letting Nolla Health’s AI system scan a user’s face and issue a prescription directly.
The service is launching as a pilot program with gradually loosening physician oversight. Two physicians will approve each AI-generated prescription before they’re issued for the first 100 patients, but will start reviewing them only after they’re prescribed for up to 500 patients. “After that, physicians review a sample of at least 10% of prescriptions every month, plus every case involving an escalation or side effect,” Nolla Health says.
Several other healthcare companies are experimenting with AI-generated prescriptions in Utah, which started allowing AI systems to renew certain medications earlier this year. But Nolla Health says it’s the first in the country to issue initial prescriptions, rather than renewals. “The pilot is designed to complement, not replace, physicians,” Nolla Health writes in its press release. “By handling routine, low-acuity cases, Nolla Derm frees dermatologists to focus on complex, high-risk patients.”
The program will cost $4.99 / month, and only applies to Utah residents who are 18 years of age or older and have mild-to-moderate acne. Nolla Health says it will direct users to a physician if its AI system cannot “confidently select a treatment.” The startup’s AI can currently prescribe eight different skin treatments, according to Bloomberg.

articles.title: Hackers steal 8 million citizens' records from Danish government database | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Danish government has confirmed that its central database of citizens’ data was breached and most of its contents were stolen. The data breach affects some 8 million citizens and residents of Denmark, including people living abroad and the deceased.
In a statement, Danish minister Christina Egelund said the breach of the country’s Central Person Register (CPR) was a “serious incident,” which allowed hackers to steal names, addresses, Danish social security numbers, and other information.
The CPR is a government database of Danish citizens’ information, including their government-issued identity number for paying taxes and accessing other services. Denmark’s current population is about 6 million people, but the database includes records for about 11 million people, with some of the data going back decades.
The Danish government would not say who is behind the breach, which happened in September but was discovered on October 2. However, it said the unauthorized access was obtained by “abusing a Danish company’s lawful access to search for information in the CPR system.” (Some companies in Denmark have access to the CPR for verifying people’s information with the government.)
The data breach is thought to be the biggest in the country’s history. It follows similar cyberattacks targeting government national identity databases, including a 2016 breach affecting millions of Turkish citizens and several exposures of national ID cards and data spilled from India’s national Aadhaar database of citizens.

articles.title: How far away can a Wi-Fi extender be from your router? - Engadget
articles.text:
How far away can a Wi-Fi extender be from your router?
Wi-Fi extenders can be finicky, and placement matters more than you might think.
No matter how many antennas your Wi-Fi router has, its signal can only go so far before it starts to decline and eventually fades entirely. While that's normal, it can leave your home with Wi-Fi dead zones: areas where the wireless signal is weak or nonexistent. This is where Wi-Fi extenders can swoop in and help — to an extent.
Top Wi-Fi extenders, as their name implies, capture and extend the reach of your router's signal coverage. This makes them a simple and cost-effective solution for covering dead zones and weak spots, particularly in smaller homes. But similar to your router, a Wi-Fi extender has its limits. The biggest is that it simply re-broadcasts the signal it receives, regardless of whether it's weak or strong. In other words, you have to place it at just the right position to cover the dead zone while still receiving a strong signal from your router.
The prevailing placement recommendation is halfway between the device or dead zone and router. However, proper Wi-Fi extender placement also varies depending on how your space is built and what's inside it.
Understanding a Wi-Fi extender's effective range
Under ideal conditions, the halfway point usually works out to placing the extender around 25 to 40 feet from the router if it has external antennas. For models with internal antennas, suitable placement is 20 to 35 feet from the router.
The right positioning is vital because unlike a router, which only has to broadcast signals, an extender has to receive and then re-broadcast the signal it gets. Many Wi-Fi extenders use the same channel to receive and send data, which cuts their available bandwidth in half since they can't listen and speak at the same time. Bad placement worsens the effects of this.
Depending on how your space is built, finding a good spot might be difficult. The distance figures above assume a strong router signal and few obstacles. But barriers like thick concrete walls, brick, floors, metal surfaces, microwaves and even baby monitors all weaken or interfere with the signal. You'll need to account for those when deciding where to place the extender. If a brick wall or floor stands between your router and the dead zone, you'll likely need to place the extender closer to the router than the halfway point.
The best way to find the right spot is by letting the extender guide you. Most extenders have lights that show the strength of the signal they're receiving. Start by setting it up near the router, then gradually move it toward the dead zone while monitoring its signal LED. Do this until you find a balanced point where the extender covers the dead zone while still having a solid connection to the router. For best reception, keep it about four feet off the ground, roughly level with your router, and position the antennas straight up (perpendicular to the floor).
When a Wi-Fi extender is not enough: wired or mesh
Sometimes, Wi-Fi extenders aren't worth it because you can't get good performance from them anywhere. This is especially common in large homes. At that point, you have two other options.
The first is to go wired. Set your extender to access point mode, then run an Ethernet cable from it to your router. Going wired bypasses signal degradation and interference, and lets you place the extender right in the dead zone, all while keeping your router's bandwidth intact. Keep in mind that Ethernet cables have a maximum effective length of 100 meters (328 feet), and not all extenders have an Ethernet port or support access point mode.
The second option is getting one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems. If the Ethernet cable didn't help or you're considering a second extender, this is the way to go. A mesh network uses nodes placed around your space to extend your router's signal, covering dead zones. Unlike Wi-Fi extenders, which create a separate "EXT" network you have to connect to, mesh systems keep everything on the same network while smart routing automatically connects your device to the strongest node. They handle signals traveling through unfriendly surfaces and spaces better than extenders, plus tri-band systems avoid halving your bandwidth.
Mesh systems are more expensive than Wi-Fi extenders, but their superior performance and reliability make them a better solution.

articles.title: ‘Panic-inducing’: Bernie Moreno takes on Anthropic’s Dario Amodei
articles.text:
Republican senator Bernie Moreno has accused Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei of taking an “alarmist approach” to AI. He did so in a letter sent on Monday, ahead of Anthropic’s expected stock market listing. Axios first reported the letter.
“I do not understand how you can ask them to invest their hard-earned savings in Anthropic’s continued development while warning those same Americans that your product could ultimately lead to their extinction,” Moreno wrote.
The Ohio senator calls AI “super intelligence”, or SI, throughout the letter. That follows President Trump’s order for US agencies to rename the technology.
Coxon, Hubinger and Amodei
Moreno cited Jacob Coxon, the researcher who quit Anthropic in September and said AI companies were “gambling with our lives”. He also quoted Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger, who put the chance that AI kills all humans within the next decade at more than 10%.
The letter quotes Amodei telling CNN that he agrees with Coxon “on far more than I disagree with him”. Moreno also wrote that Amodei has put the chance of SI going “really, really badly” at 25%. These statements show that Amodei’s “instinct is to wreak havoc on the public SI discourse”, the senator wrote. He said the “panic-inducing commentary” does not tell Americans how the technology can defend against the threats it warns about.
The IPO and China
Moreno wrote that investors are discussing a valuation for Anthropic of close to $2tn, about 42 times its revenue. Trading could start as soon as this month, he said. Anthropic’s IPO prospectus has already warned investors about risks from US government action.
The senator said the focus on worst-case outcomes risks crowding out debate on national security and on keeping the US, not China, in the lead. He called Amodei’s signature on the White House accord on super intelligence “a notable first step”.
“We must address the risks associated with frontier SI. Doing so does not require halting its development or surrendering American technological dominance,” Moreno wrote.
The letter is the latest from an ally of President Trump aimed at Amodei, Axios reported.
