articles.title: Giá xăng dầu hôm nay 5/10: Thế giới xu hướng tăng, trong nước trái chiều
articles.text:
Giá dầu thế giới hôm nay
Mở cửa phiên giao dịch đầu tuần này (5/10), giá dầu thế giới có xu hướng đi lên.
Dữ liệu từ Oilprice cho hay, vào lúc 6h49' ngày 5/10 (giờ Việt Nam), giá dầu Brent được niêm yết ở mức 102,7 USD/thùng, tăng 0,42% so với phiên liền trước. Còn giá dầu WTI được giao dịch ở mức 91,16 USD/thùng, tăng 0,05% so với phiên liền trước.
Trong tuần trước, giá dầu thế giới biến động trái chiều, giá dầu Brent tăng 0,11% trong khi giá dầu WTI giảm 1,6%.
Giá dầu Brent đóng cửa tuần qua ở mức 102,3 USD/thùng, còn giá dầu WTI kết tuần trước ở mức 91,11 USD/thùng.
Ở phiên giao dịch cuối cùng của tuần trước, giá dầu thế giới giảm sau khi các lãnh đạo châu Âu đồng ý với đề nghị của Tổng thống Mỹ Donald Trump về việc xả kho dự trữ dầu diesel nhằm hạ giá nhiên liệu.
Trước đó, ông Donald Trump cho biết đang cân nhắc lệnh cấm xuất khẩu diesel của Mỹ.
"Nếu Mỹ áp lệnh cấm xuất khẩu diesel, châu Âu sẽ là một trong những khu vực chịu ảnh hưởng nặng nề nhất”, Phil Flynn, chuyên gia phân tích cấp cao tại Price Futures Group, cho hay.
Trong khi đó, thị trường vẫn nhận được những tín hiệu hỗ trợ từ nguồn cung dầu thô.
Trong một báo cáo mới đây, Ngân hàng Barclays (Anh) cho biết dòng chảy dầu thô từ Trung Đông đang cải thiện, các yếu tố cơ bản của thị trường vật chất vẫn ở trạng thái tích cực.
Ngân hàng này đã nâng dự báo giá dầu Brent trong quý IV thêm 20 USD/thùng, lên 115 USD/thùng, đồng thời nâng dự báo giá dầu Brent trung bình năm 2026 lên 100 USD/thùng.
Giá xăng dầu trong nước hôm nay
Giá bán của các mặt hàng xăng dầu phổ biến tại thị trường trong nước vào hôm nay (5/10) được áp dụng như sau:
Theo kỳ điều hành ngày 1/10, giá bán lẻ xăng E5RON92 tăng 172 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 26.569 đồng/lít.
Giá xăng E10RON95-III cũng tăng 102 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 27.189 đồng/lít.
Trái lại, giá dầu diesel 0.05S giảm 780 đồng/lít, giá bán không cao hơn 29.717 đồng/lít.
Trong khi giá bán dầu mazut 180CST 3.5S tăng 919 đồng/kg, giá bán không cao hơn 20.391 đồng/kg.
Theo dữ liệu từ Bộ Công Thương, giá bán lẻ xăng dầu tại Việt Nam hiện ở mức thấp hơn so với các nước có chung đường biên giới.
Liên bộ Công Thương - Tài chính đang tiếp tục theo dõi sát diễn biến thị trường để thông báo giá xăng dầu phù hợp với diễn biến thị trường và kịp thời đề xuất Chính phủ, Thủ tướng các giải pháp bình ổn giá xăng dầu.

articles.title: All the drama around AI’s takeover of mathematics
articles.text:
This past year, OpenAI, Anthropic, and other labs have announced breakthroughs on numerous long-standing mathematical problems, in some cases pushing well beyond what researchers expected current systems to be capable of — including resolving one of the famous Millennium Prize problems. But in classic Silicon Valley style, AI labs are moving fast and breaking things, barreling through the discipline with all the grace of a runaway bulldozer. Results that might normally have been celebrated have instead sparked backlash. AI labs say they are learning from earlier mistakes. Whether those promises bear fruit remains to be seen.
Read on below for the latest updates in the AI takeover of mathematics.
- OpenAI keeps bulldozing mathematicians In a chaotic few months, OpenAI has demonstrated it can do two things with remarkable consistency: make impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, then colossally screw up announcing them. OpenAI is now trying to do better. Somehow, it has botched that too. OpenAI’s latest attempt to repair fractured relations with a mathematical community it has repeatedly alienated is to consult a new independent advisory group of elite practitioners. But mathematicians speaking to The Verge, including one of the group’s members, describe a messy and confusing affair bearing many of the hallmarks of OpenAI’s previous rushed forays into mathematics, suggesting the company has learned little from its mistakes. And then there’s the daunting task the group has been handed first: helping coordinate the release of scores more results OpenAI says its unreleased model has produced, the prospect of which is already stirring dread among researchers over what this looming tidal wave of breakthroughs could do to their field. Read Article >
- OpenAI wants to consult elite mathematicians about how to not fumble again After turning a string of spectacular mathematical results into a reputational crisis, OpenAI is consulting human mathematicians to help it figure out a less disastrous path forward. On Monday, the company announced a new independent panel of mathematicians tasked with advising it and other AI companies on their interactions with mathematical research and the wider mathematics community, including how new results are presented and released. Its abrupt arrival caught many mathematicians by surprise. Researchers told The Verge the group is a good first step, but many said they were left with basic questions about what it will actually do, how much influence it will have, and whether OpenAI will actually listen to it, as well as concerns over whether such a small group of prominent researchers can represent the wider mathematical community. Read Article >
- OpenAI just wants to win OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement. Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win. Read Article >
- Mathematicians want proof OpenAI didn’t use their work Another researcher is challenging OpenAI about the data driving its increasingly impressive array of mathematical discoveries. Just days after a bitter row erupted over whether the company’s models benefited from unpublished work, a second mathematician has come forward accusing the AI giant of unethical and “dishonest” behavior and a lack of transparency about the origins of its training data. In a series of posts on Mastodon, mathematician Andreas Thom raised concerns that interactions he and his colleagues had had with the ChatGPT chatbot before OpenAI’s triumphant announcement may have contributed to its success in the field. One of the 10 results OpenAI announced with great fanfare last month involved Thom’s area of expertise, so-called non-sofic groups, and OpenAI acknowledged that their result built heavily on previous work by Thom and fellow mathematician Gábor Kun. Read Article >
- OpenAI’s sly mathematical breakthrough sends a chill through academia OpenAI’s announcement Tuesday that it has solved one of mathematics’ legendary Millennium Prize problems should have been a moment of triumph. The result is both an undeniable achievement and a striking demonstration of just how rapidly AI is transforming mathematics. But before it was even formally announced, the breakthrough had been complicated by the unusual circumstances that prompted OpenAI to pursue the problem: After hearing other researchers were making progress, it seems to have thrown its considerable resources into a last-minute effort to beat them to the punch. The ensuing controversy has surfaced allegations of scooping, spying, and flagrant violations of long-standing academic norms that researchers fear could have a chilling effect on the field. As Abhishek Saha, a mathematics professor at Queen Mary University of London, explains it, OpenAI has engaged in the “kind of things that mathematicians will generally not do.” Read Article >
- Drama swirls around OpenAI’s legendary mathematical milestone OpenAI says it found a solution to a major math problem that has remained unsolved for around 90 years, as reported earlier by The New York Times and Wired. In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI announced that it discovered a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem — which relates to the flow of liquid and gas — using an internal AI model more powerful than the newly released GPT-6 Astra alongside 10,000 concurrent agents. The Navier-Stokes problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million reward for solving. OpenAI says it started training the internal AI model on August 28th, which has “exhibited unprecedented performance in our benchmarks, including mathematics.” The solution is a big breakthrough for the mathematics community, but it doesn’t come without controversy. Read Article >
- Welcome to the AI crisis in math Today on Decoder, I’m talking with Robert Hart, The Verge’s London-based AI reporter, about what AI is doing to the field of mathematics and the existential crisis many lead mathematicians are having about it. OpenAI just published a set of solutions to longstanding problems in math that went off like a bombshell in the field. It caused a huge debate in the math community, and Rob spent some time talking to some of the most accomplished mathematicians of our time about it. Read Article >
- The AI takeover of mathematics has begun Mathematician James Maynard has spent a lot of time this past year “soul searching.” A professor at the University of Oxford and winner of the prestigious Fields Medal, Maynard told The Verge he’s been grappling with the future of his field as the traditionally slow-moving discipline hurries to adapt to AI. Days before we spoke, OpenAI revealed it had produced the solutions to 10 long-standing mathematics problems, some of which had confounded academics for decades. Like generative AI used to produce text and images or propose ideas in science and medicine, the technology learns patterns and connections from the vast amount of material it’s trained on and uses them to create something new. Applied to mathematics, that can mean combining known results, methods, and tools in new ways to attack a problem, sometimes drawing links between disparate fields or resurfacing concepts buried in academic literature. Read Article >

articles.title: Researchers are tracking a Chinese AI 'agent fleet' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
A new fleet of AI agents is making its presence felt on the internet. On Sunday, a group of independent researchers posted preliminary findings about the agents, observing that they seem to be running on Tencent’s infrastructure and targeting Alibaba’s map service, Amap.
Researchers, however, resisted the term “swarm,” noting that there seems to be little coordination between their different queries. “‘Agent fleet,’ not ‘swarm:’” one researcher wrote in the preliminary report, “many parallel agents on the same kind of task, with no sign of communication between them.”
The agents were discovered by monitoring traffic to the domain-scanning service urlquery, a technique that previously revealed long-running activity by OpenAI agents. AI agents often use urlquery to load websites that they cannot access directly, leaving a record of their activities that can be valuable to researchers.
In this case, the record showed queries to Alibaba’s Amap service, seeking directions to different entrances of various public places, including a park, a zoo, and a hospital.
The research is ongoing and so few details are available, but the behavior shows how persistent AI agent activity has become on the internet. In the wake of the Hugging Face incident, many researchers are actively monitoring for rogue agent activity on the internet. Much of that activity has been easy to find because agents tend to use the same techniques and make little effort to conceal themselves.
In this case, the agents don’t seem to have been doing anything more nefarious than side-stepping Alibaba’s API rules — but we may not always be so lucky.

articles.title: Google's Fitbit Edge leaks out with a screen and Pixel 11 colors - Engadget
articles.text:
Google's Fitbit Edge leaks out with a screen and Pixel 11 colors
It could offer a seven-day battery life, altimeter and limited support for apps like Google Maps.
We knew that Google was likely coming out with a mid-range Fitbit model that slots between the Fitbit Air and the Pixel Watch 5, thanks to ads that surfaced earlier this year. Now we're seeing the first leak of the upcoming fitness tracker called the Fitbit Edge thanks to Android Headlines. It could be a replacement for the Fitbit Charge last seen in 2023, as it's equipped with a similar small screen and expected to have features like a GPS and notifications.
The leaks suggest that the Fitbit Edge will offer a seven-day battery life, GPS, altimeter and limited app support for apps like Google Maps and YouTube music. That will make it a more powerful Fitbit Air or a Pixel Watch 5 "lite," but one that runs on iOS as well as Android, unlike the Android-only Watch 5. It could come in multiple colors seen on Pixel 11 smartphones, like Rose Peach and Olive.
The new device is likely to arrive in time for the holiday 2026 season. The price is anyone's guess but it could be a touch more than the older Fitbit Charge, which cost between $129 and $179. That would put it around $150 to $200, slotting it neatly between the $100 Fitbit Air and $400 Pixel Watch 5.

articles.title: Texas city wants $2.3M for public records on police Flock use
articles.text:
A Fort Worth suburb has told a privacy group it would cost $2.3M to release records on how its police use Flock number plate cameras, a figure reached by estimating 14 years of labour at $15 an hour. Under the EU’s law enforcement directive the same information has to be logged as a matter of course and handed to the data protection authority on request.
A Texas city has told a privacy group it would cost $2.3M to see how its police use Flock cameras. It reached that figure by estimating 14 years of labour at $15 an hour. Another handed over 400,000 pages for nothing.
North Richland Hills, a Fort Worth suburb, said searching about a terabyte of communications about errors, misuse and effectiveness would take that long, as the Texas Tribune reported. Sealy charged nothing. Irving asked $70,000 for records Carrollton released free.
A Houston television station, KPRC, was quoted $121,000.
The records are how anyone finds out anything.
An audit set off by a USA Today request caught a Lufkin officer searching police databases about his former girlfriend, her family and men she had dated. Zachary Anthony Klein pleaded guilty on 30 September to 100 felony counts and drew five years. We reported his indictment in August, when records showed 45,318 searches across 210 days.
One plate had been queried 3,470 times.
Texas has about 13,000 Flock cameras, part of a network of more than 100,000 across America. Fifty-nine agencies use the transparency portals Flock offers, covering 2,600 of those cameras, and 16 publish their search records.
Sixteen, out of hundreds of agencies running the cameras.
The state’s own police force is going the other way, after Governor Greg Abbott froze state funding in August. The Department of Public Safety answered an identical request in July, limited August’s to its own searches, and has now asked the Attorney General’s Office to let it withhold the data entirely.
Europe does not obtain this by asking.
Under the EU’s law enforcement directive, police systems must log every consultation and disclosure, recording the justification, the date and time, who searched and who received the data, and controllers must hand those logs to the data protection authority on request. There is no fee and no labour estimate. The logs go to the regulator rather than to the public, which is a different bargain and not a better one.
Britain’s national standards for number plate recognition, updated in July, require audit trails covering logins and every successful and failed search, make access to the audit trail itself auditable, and delete national read data after 90 days.
A federal judge in Oklahoma ruled last week that a warrantless Flock search was unconstitutional mass surveillance, and 404 Media counts more than 100,000 such searches a month.

articles.title: I Look Forward to Stepping on This Smart Scale Every Week
articles.text:
I’m going to be honest from the start: No, you probably don’t need a $600 scale in your bathroom if you are just doing occasional weigh-ins. Hell, I don’t even know that elite athletes need to make this kind of extreme outlay even if they need to periodically check on how their training is going.
But I’m going to make the case for the Withings BodyScan 2 anyway. After spending several months with the device, the scale and its ecosystem have forced me to dig deeper into my health than ever before. At this point, I’m not sure I could go back to an older-model scale—even a very smart one like the original Withings Body Smart, which I used for years.
Getting a Handle on Health
There’s not much to distinguish the BodyScan 2 hardware from other smart scales aside from its handlebars, an indication that this device belongs to the now-burgeoning full-body scanner or body composition scale category. The device is, however, sleeker than most of its competition, featuring a svelte handle that somehow finds room for a small color LCD screen without the need for any extra bulk. All of your body metrics are showcased on this screen in real time, as they’re being measured, alongside any quick tips from Withings about how to get the best reading each time you hop on.
The unit offers two types of weigh-ins. Daily scans take about 30 seconds and include weight, an estimate of muscle and fat percentage (whole body and segmented across torso, arms, legs, and viscera), an estimate of basal metabolic rate, vascular age, and pulse wave velocity—though only a portion of these measurements are displayed live on the display.

articles.title: Wikipedia operator says OpenAI’s ‘rogue’ bots may be linked to a May outage
articles.text:
Following many recent disclosures about AI agents accessing third-party websites and services, the Wikimedia Foundation, which hosts Wikipedia, says that it “can confirm that we have discovered some activity” by “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms.
Wikipedia operator says OpenAI’s ‘rogue’ bots may be linked to a May outage
The Wikimedia Foundation believes OpenAI agents edited wikis, tried to ‘exploit’ a notetaking tool, and made ‘millions’ of automated API requests.
The activity includes edits to Wikimedia wikis, “unsuccessful attempts” to “exploit” the Etherpad note-taking tool that the Wikimedia Foundation hosts, and heavy traffic that the foundation says “may” have contributed to a partial outage that happened in May, according to a blog post. However, the Wikimedia Foundation says it didn’t find evidence that its systems were “used for coordination among agents” (recently, OpenAI bots reportedly hijacked a German wiki site to coordinate) or evidence of systems or data being compromised.
Here’s Wikimedia’s summary of what it saw:
Wiki editing: We’ve identified edits to Wikimedia wikis that we believe are from AI agents operated by OpenAI. These edits were not published to pages with visibility to general readers; almost all of them were testing edits in “sandbox” areas of the wiki. It also included a few edits to the configuration for a citation tool, which we believe were potentially malicious edits that were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services. While Wikipedia policies allow bots to edit when they are disclosed and approved by the community, none of those approvals were sought in these incidents.
Etherpad probing and use: Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made some unsuccessful attempts to compromise our public Etherpad, a note-taking tool we host as a community service. Agents unsuccessfully tried to use it to fetch data from other websites as a proxy. Other agents also likely operated by OpenAI took notes about their tasks, though this did not appear to turn into coordination.
Excessive data downloading: Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made millions of automated requests to our public APIs to access the knowledge on Wikimedia projects, crawled millions of pages (mainly from our projects Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons), and made hundreds of thousands of data queries to the Wikidata Query Service (WQDS). This traffic may have contributed to a partial outage on WQDS in May.
“The open web is a public good,” the Wikimedia Foundation says. “We should not allow this behavior to become the ‘new normal’ for the people or organizations that maintain it.”
“We appreciate the detailed findings Wikimedia shared with us,” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri says in a statement. “We’re working with them as we review and analyze the activity they identified along with our overall investigation, and we’ll continue to share relevant information as that work progresses.” OpenAI’s investigation hasn’t been able to verify if its bots contributed to the May outage, according to Pusateri.
Update, October 5th: Added statement from OpenAI.

articles.title: Meta, TikTok and X challenge Ofcom over Online Safety Act data demands
articles.text:
Meta, TikTok and X are challenging Ofcom in court over its data demands under the UK’s Online Safety Act, Reuters reported on Monday. The challenge is one of the first brought under the 2023 law.
In February, Ofcom sent the companies information notices, according to Paul Sandle’s report for Reuters. The notices asked for detailed content moderation figures, such as how many posts the platforms removed or made less visible. They also asked how many users had seen harmful content.
The Online Safety Act sets tougher standards for platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X. It aims to protect children from harmful and illegal content. Ofcom can fine companies up to 10% of their global turnover for the most serious breaches.
‘The most burdensome’ request
The three companies say the notices create an unprecedented regulatory burden, Reuters reported. A witness statement submitted by X called the notice:
“The most burdensome information request X has received from any regulator in any jurisdiction.”
Meta said in court filings that Ofcom wanted “wide-ranging and granular information” about seven of its services. It said the request had no clearly defined regulatory purpose. TikTok said Ofcom had bypassed a separate monitoring regime that has its own safeguards.
Ofcom’s answer
Ofcom said it genuinely needs the information to judge whether the new regime is working. It also said it narrowed the scope of its request before the notices took effect.
“Parliament has charged us with the job of regulating an industry that has been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years,” an Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement.
The hearing ends on Wednesday. A separate challenge from Meta should reach court next week, Reuters said. It concerns how Ofcom calculates Online Safety Act bills.
Ofcom already has open investigations under the law, including one into TikTok over child safety and one into Telegram.

articles.title: What are the benefits of having a second monitor? - Engadget
articles.text:
What are the benefits of having a second monitor?
Two screens means more real estate to run apps without having to switch between them all the time.
Upgrading to dual monitors is the best workflow upgrade you can make, with some studies indicating that it can boost productivity and satisfaction. Whether it's for multitasking, to expand a split-screen view, gaming or everyday office tasks, there's a lot of value in this setup.
While you might think dual screens are mostly for gamers or those who work in computer-intensive fields like music and video production or accounting, that's not the case. My best friend works in insurance and uses a dual-monitor setup so she can copy and paste information from one document to another instead of switching tabs, or put her Teams chat on one monitor while working on the other. She added that "Dragging and dropping documents is so easy." Bottom line: there are plenty of benefits for anyone who regularly multitasks.
Usability advantages of a second monitor
The most obvious reason to set up two of the best monitors is being able to spread your work across multiple screens. The app I use most on my MacBook is split-screen, so I can write on one half while conducting web research or going through PDF briefs on the other. The benefit of having two full-sized monitors to do this, versus half a screen with small font, is easy to realize. Creative professionals or data analysts, meanwhile, can expand the screen real estate and see more at once. Professions like traders and programmers may benefit from three or even four monitors. But for most people, two is the sweet spot.
It's worthwhile for any kind of multitasking. I always have tons of tabs open on my computer and consistently use two separate web browsers. You can work on two tasks at the same time, like tweaking your resume on one monitor while hunting through job listings on the other. A second monitor can be home for communication apps or other mostly-static information you want to keep an eye on, like your email inbox.
Beyond text-based documents like word processing and spreadsheets, two monitors are great for gamers. You can play on one screen and use the second to manage game recording, chat with your streaming audience, access Discord and more without having to leave the game. During a video call, you can take notes on one display while looking at your team on the other. Or if you're making a how-to video, you could have a script open on one monitor while you perform the steps on the second.
Dual monitor organization and tips
Having a second monitor allows for better organization, both on your desk and the screens. I sometimes print reference documents to view them separately. A second monitor would eliminate the need to do this, saving paper (and clutter). By not relying on a phone or tablet as a second screen, you avoid the risk of getting caught up in mobile distractions.
It's worth noting that you don't necessarily need a high-end second monitor. Specs like high refresh rate are more important for the display you're looking at most of the time. For a second one you use only when necessary, a more affordable monitor is fine. Ideally, you should find a second monitor that is the same size as your first for a seamless look. It should also have the same pixel density to ensure matching text and image scaling. Finally, get mounting hardware to situate them at the same level.
Be aware of how far you should sit from your monitor, as well as the proper eye height, and set them up accordingly. You'll need to find a tidy way to connect both monitors to your computer, which requires two video outputs and the appropriate cables. Then, adjust display settings like brightness and contrast as needed.
If you're using a laptop, you might need to configure it to stay running when you close the lid if you aren't using it as one of your displays. Most modern MacBooks can support at least two monitors, for instance.
A second monitor might not be something you use all the time. But having it there when you need it can be, as my friend noted, a "complete game-changer." Being able to look at one program while working in another one saves you from constantly switching app windows and lets you keep an eye on what's most important.

articles.title: Trung Quốc gom mua hàng triệu tấn gạo của Việt Nam, chỉ sau một quốc gia
articles.text:
Theo báo cáo mới nhất của Bộ Nông nghiệp và Môi trường, trong tháng 9, nước ta xuất khẩu 377.400 tấn gạo, thu về 205,6 triệu USD.
Lũy kế 9 tháng năm 2026, các doanh nghiệp nước ta xuất khẩu khoảng 6,4 triệu tấn gạo, trị giá 3,11 tỷ USD. So với cùng kỳ năm ngoái, xuất khẩu gạo giảm 6,1% về khối lượng và giảm 10,9% về giá trị.
Giá gạo xuất khẩu bình quân 9 tháng ước đạt 484,8 USD/tấn, giảm 5,1% so với cùng kỳ năm 2025.
Về cơ cấu thị trường xuất khẩu, số liệu cập nhật đến hết tháng 8/2026 cho thấy Philippines vẫn là khách hàng lớn nhất mua gạo Việt Nam với thị phần chiếm 40,9%. Tuy nhiên, xuất khẩu gạo sang thị trường này đang giảm 16,8%.
Đáng chú ý, từ vị trí thứ tư của cùng kỳ năm 2025, năm nay Trung Quốc vươn lên vị trí thị trường xuất khẩu gạo lớn thứ hai của Việt Nam, chiếm 17,4% tổng lượng xuất khẩu trong 8 tháng.
Theo đó, chỉ trong 8 tháng, quốc gia tỷ dân này đã chi gần 505 triệu USD để mua khoảng 1,03 triệu tấn gạo của Việt Nam. Trong khi cùng kỳ năm ngoái, Trung Quốc chỉ nhập hơn 565.000 tấn, giá trị 286,7 triệu USD.
Bộ Nông nghiệp và Môi trường cho biết nhu cầu gạo tấm từ Trung Quốc tăng mạnh, chủ yếu phục vụ sản xuất thức ăn chăn nuôi.
Trong 8 tháng năm 2026, xuất khẩu gạo của Việt Nam sang Iraq tăng đột biến 98,9 lần so với cùng kỳ năm ngoái. Dù vậy, kim ngạch xuất khẩu sang thị trường này vẫn còn khá khiêm tốn, chỉ dừng ở mức gần 14 triệu USD.
Đánh giá về cung - cầu, thương mại và giá gạo niên vụ 2026-2027, Bộ Nông nghiệp và Môi trường cho rằng sự phục hồi xuất khẩu sang Iraq cho thấy dư địa đa dạng hóa thị trường vẫn còn, cần được khai thác chủ động, bền vững hơn trong các tháng cuối năm.
Bên cạnh đó, Bộ này cũng nhận định mức độ tập trung vào thị trường Philippines và Trung Quốc tăng lên, chiếm hơn 64% tổng lượng xuất khẩu - là lợi thế trong ngắn hạn, song cũng làm gia tăng rủi ro phụ thuộc vào một số thị trường. Bộ cho rằng cần từng bước đa dạng hóa thị trường xuất khẩu.
Theo tính toán của Hiệp hội Lương thực Việt Nam, tháng 10 nước ta dự kiến xuất khẩu 400.000 tấn; tháng 11 và tháng 12 lần lượt khoảng 220.000 và 268.300 tấn.
Dự báo tổng lượng gạo xuất khẩu cả năm 2026 đạt gần 7,74 triệu tấn, kim ngạch khoảng 3,94 tỷ USD, giảm 4% về giá trị so với năm 2025, do giá xuất khẩu bình quân các tháng đầu năm ở mức thấp.
Theo dự báo, nếu đạt sản lượng xuất khẩu gần 7,74 triệu tấn, Việt Nam có thể tiếp tục đứng thứ hai thế giới về lượng gạo xuất khẩu, chỉ sau Ấn Độ.
Triển vọng giá gạo xuất khẩu trong những tháng cuối năm được hỗ trợ bởi một số yếu tố. Cân đối cung - cầu gạo thế giới niên vụ 2026-2027 được dự báo chuyển sang thâm hụt, trong khi thương mại gạo toàn cầu có thể đạt mức kỷ lục.
Philippines mới đây khẳng định không áp dụng lệnh tạm dừng nhập khẩu trong năm 2026 và tiếp tục nhập khẩu để tăng dự trữ. Đây là tin vui bởi Việt Nam hiện chiếm phần lớn tổng lượng nhập khẩu của thị trường này.
Thị trường Trung Quốc ghi nhận tăng trưởng đột phá về lượng, mở ra dư địa lớn cho phân khúc gạo nguyên liệu, gạo tấm và gạo nếp.
Ở phân khúc gạo chất lượng cao, phát thải thấp có chứng nhận đạt giá trên 1.000 USD/tấn tại thị trường Nhật Bản, EU, Australia, khẳng định dư địa nâng giá trị gia tăng của gạo Việt Nam.
Nguồn cung toàn cầu cũng có thể chịu tác động từ diễn biến El Niño, tình hình gió mùa tại Ấn Độ và diện tích gieo cấy lúa vụ Kharif. Bên cạnh đó, căng thẳng địa chính trị tại Trung Đông có thể gây sức ép lên chi phí năng lượng và vận tải biển.

articles.title: Hyundai CEO says only a ‘level playing field’ can minimize damage from China
articles.text:
There’s been a lot of doom and gloom from the auto industry lately when the subject of China comes up. Automaker CEOs, in particular, warn that allowing low-cost, high-tech Chinese electric vehicles to be sold in the US would effectively spell the end of their businesses.
Hyundai CEO says only a ‘level playing field’ can minimize damage from China
Hyundai CEO José Muñoz says the US could be overrun like Europe without protections in place.
Hyundai CEO José Muñoz is not as pessimistic as some of his counterparts. He says he’s confident the right mix of protectionist policies and improvements on the product side can keep China at bay. Even though his company is feeling the squeeze from China, Muñoz isn’t ready to throw in the towel. But he also acknowledges that China could flood the US with affordable imports without established protections in place.
“As long as there is a level playing field for everybody,” Muñoz said at the reveal of the new 2027 Hyundai Tucson in New York City last week. “That’s all we ask, right? We compete everywhere in the world, and then we have seen that in the markets where that position is respected, so it’s really good for us.”
Chinese automakers have expanded rapidly in Europe, gobbling up market share and damaging domestic brands like Volkswagen, Volvo, and Mercedes by offering vehicles at much lower prices. US automakers warn the same could be true for them if China were allowed to import its vehicles here.
“We compete everywhere in the world, and then we have seen that in the markets where that position is respected, so it’s really good for us.”
— José Muñoz
Steep tariffs and laws that prohibit the sale of cars with software from China have basically made it impossible to sell Chinese vehicles in the US. But in recent months, the dam appears to be weakening. President Donald Trump has said several times that he would be open to Chinese automakers building manufacturing plants in the US if they hire American workers. And experts across the board believe it’s only a matter of time before China finds a way to sell its cars in the US.
But if Chinese brands eventually set up manufacturing inside North America or enter via partner channels, it’s not clear whether Hyundai has a defensive strategy ready. I asked Muñoz whether his company had begun to plan for the eventuality of Chinese imports available in the US market. He said it had not.
“We don’t develop strategies specifically because of the Chinese or because of other types of consumers, or other types of competitors,” he said. “We are always trying to do better.”
If Hyundai has any strategy, Muñoz added, it’s vertical integration: bringing down costs by making its tech and components. “This allows us to be more competitive,” he said. “Better quality over cost.”
“We don’t develop strategies specifically because of the Chinese or because of other types of consumers, or other types of competitors.”
Muñoz cited Hyundai’s $5.8 billion investment in Louisiana to produce green steel as an example of the company’s efforts to vertically integrate in the US. Hyundai expects the investment to provide better, more competitive, and more environmentally friendly steel. He says the same philosophy applies to software and other technologies that Hyundai wants to develop internally.
“So there is always room to do better,” he continued. “So if the Chinese competitor were to enter in the market, we would see what would happen, but I don’t know, I don’t have a crystal ball. I just look around, for example, Europe, and see what has happened, and then you may expect similar type of behaviors.”
Chinese vehicles sold in Europe are on average about 30 percent cheaper than comparable European-made rival models, even when factoring in EU import tariffs. The US has already fallen behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption, after Trump and Republicans in Congress eliminated federal subsidies. In Europe, EVs account for over 20 percent of sales; in China, it’s over 60 percent. In the US, it’s less than 6 percent.
Political polarization certainly plays a role in depressing sales, as does inadequate charging infrastructure. But the lack of affordable electric models is regularly cited as the biggest barrier to adoption in the US. On that front, Muñoz thinks the US can still catch up.
“I think the American market is the most competitive in the world,” he said, noting that Hyundai still records robust EV sales here. That may be true, but the company’s hybrids are what’s keeping its EV business afloat. Hyundai has added hybrids to a wide range of vehicles, including its top-selling Tucson.
Unlike other automakers, Hyundai hasn’t retreated from EVs. It continues to sell its Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9 here in the US, as well as a growing number of hybrids. In fact, the Hyundai Group recently surpassed Honda to claim second place in US hybrid sales behind Toyota.
Muñoz acknowledged that the US was still catching up to China’s dominance in EV batteries. Hyundai operates a battery manufacturing joint venture with SK On in Georgia near its massive Metaplant, where it builds all of its EVs and hybrids.
“Obviously if you don’t have the critical mass, the volume, it’s very difficult to be competitive,” he said. “One of the biggest pieces of cost is the battery. That is the key element, right? But there is a lot of production of batteries in the United States with some of the best global manufacturers. So I’m not concerned.”

articles.title: Omega Has New Bond Watches Even if There Isn’t a New James Bond
articles.text:
It's been five years since James Bond was on the silver screen in No Time to Die. For fans of the secret agent, the wait has been arduous, made even harder by the fact that Amazon, which now owns the franchise, still hasn't chosen a successor to Daniel Craig, let alone started filming Bond's resurrection.
But if it's seemed like a long haul for fans, just think how it has felt for Omega, which counts on a steady stream of Bond action to regularly inject lots of lovely cash into the company via watch releases linked directly to the films. Omega's last official Bond film tie-in watch was the titanium No Time to Die Seamaster prematurely launched back in 2019, ahead of the film’s then Covid-delayed release in 2021.
Considering that Swatch Group’s net profit collapsed by almost 90 percent to $32 million in 2025 (though, thankfully, things look rosier so far this year), we shouldn't be surprised that Omega isn't bothering to wait for Jeff Bezos to put his white cat down and proceed with world domination. As there's no new Bond or Bond film to work with, Omega has decided to launch 007-themed watches anyway—not just one, but an entire collection totaling six Seamaster Divers.
You can hardly blame the brand. When Omega first strapped a Seamaster to Pierce Brosnan's wrist in 1995's GoldenEye, it reportedly saw a 20-fold sales increase. In 2012, Omega's then-president Stephen Urquhart even told Variety that Omega’s sales “look like a stock market chart” that peaks during promotion of Bond films, then sinks afterward. “The films have had a very marked influence on sales,” Urquhart conceded.
The new “James Bond and Spectre” collection is themed around good and evil, with three watches bearing the “007” symbol of James Bond, and three the octopus-like motif of Spectre, the fictional global terrorist organization in the series.
The six Seamaster Diver 300M watches share the same movement. However, the two non-limited stainless-steel editions are the core pieces, available individually at $8,600 each—one with a blue aluminum dial dedicated to James Bond, and the other black for dastardly Spectre fans. Both come on a brushed mesh bracelet.
The James Bond edition has a grade 5 titanium bezel, while the Spectre edition boasts a black ceramic bezel ring to match the dial's blackened grained finish.
The remaining four Seamasters are split across two limited-edition numbered sets—one dedicated to Bond, the other to Spectre—capped at 77 boxes each. At a cool $89,800 per pair (Omega won't sell them individually), you get one stainless-steel model on a brushed mesh bracelet, and a second in platinum-gold on leather.
Each set comes in a presentation box with an additional NATO strap, strap-changing tool, cuff links, a cord bracelet, a loupe, a leather travel pouch and card holder, and papers. In the James Bond set, the strap keepers are engraved with 007; in the Spectre set, the strap keepers carry the Spectre emblem.
This collection is not the first time Omega has sought to leverage its Bond connection without a film peg. Back in May of this year, Omega unveiled the Seamaster Diver 300M Chronograph “007 First Light,” a new 44-mm chrono tied to 007 First Light, a James Bond game developed by the same studio responsible for the Hitman franchise. Originally designed as an in-game gadget, Omega turned it into a production model.
Back in 2012, there was the Seamaster James Bond 007 50th Anniversary watch with a red number 50 on the bezel. In 2019, there was an On Her Majesty's Secret Service edition Seamaster to mark 50 years of the 1969 film, limited to 7,007 pieces. Then, in 2022, Omega released a Seamaster to coincide with 60 years of Bond movies.

articles.title: TikTok adds an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout
articles.text:
TikTok is adding an AI shopping assistant and one-click checkout to its app. The two features let users buy directly from brands without leaving TikTok, the company said in an announcement at Advertising Week New York on Monday.
Buy Direct is an in-app checkout. Users can buy from a brand straight from the For You feed with one click, TikTok said. Shopping Assistant is a conversational AI agent that remembers what a user needs. It answers questions about product details, shipping, sizing and availability, and can complete the purchase in the same conversation.
TikTok said it is building the features with commerce platforms and payment providers, including Salesforce, Shopify, Shoplazza and Stripe. It did not give a launch date.
“AI is transforming how advertiser content is created and scaled,” said David Kaufman, TikTok’s global head of monetisation product partnerships.
Agents for advertisers
TikTok also announced Agentic Leads, an AI agent that holds conversations with potential customers to qualify them as sales leads. It will run in TikTok direct messages and in lead forms on advertisers’ own websites.
The TikTok Ad Network is now open to US advertisers. It lets them run campaigns across nearly 400,000 apps outside TikTok, the company said.
TikTok’s advertising tools now also work as a connector in AI platforms including Claude, Kimi, Manus, Perplexity and Replit. The connector uses the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for linking AI agents to other software. The number of advertisers using it to run campaigns has risen by more than 200% since launch, TikTok said, citing its own data for July to September.
Other updates automate search ads, pull AI-generated and creator content into one approval step, and factor costs such as affiliate commissions into TikTok Shop ad campaigns.
Shopping beyond TikTok Shop
The checkout and assistant work across the app, not only inside TikTok Shop, the marketplace TikTok launched in the US in September 2023. Market research firm eMarketer estimates TikTok Shop made about $15.8bn in US sales in 2025, TechCrunch reported. That is roughly 18% of all US social commerce.
Other companies are also building shopping into AI tools. Synchrony wants shoppers’ store cards inside ChatGPT. More than half of US consumers now use AI for shopping, according to NIQ.

articles.title: OpenAI is adding text watermarking in ChatGPT and Codex
articles.text:
An invisible, machine-readable watermark in text output is rolling out to ChatGPT and Codex, but only for users in the European Union at first.
OpenAI is adding text watermarking in ChatGPT and Codex
It’s launching textGrain watermarking in the EU, but OpenAI says it won’t be the ‘global default’ yet.
OpenAI says its textGrain watermarking “matched or exceeded” other approaches like Google DeepMind’s SynthID for text, which is also the basis for the watermarking Anthropic announced in August. Like OpenAI, Anthropic made the move to meet the requirements of the EU’s AI Act; however, not everyone was happy to learn about the addition.
OpenAI also included scores from AI benchmarks showing similar performance from watermarked and unwatermarked text. But it notes that textGrain “does not guarantee reliable detection,” and says text watermarks don’t verify accuracy, determine who owns the text, measure how much a human contributed, or prove human authorship.
Rolling out text watermarking in the EU. Over the coming weeks, we will introduce text watermarking to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users across all plans in the EU only. We are not making text watermarking a global default at launch. This regional approach gives us room to learn from real-world use and feedback.
Enabling opt-in watermarking for API customers. Starting today, API customers around the world will be able to opt in to watermarked text outputs for select models. This lets customers decide how watermarking fits their transparency obligations and the experiences they provide to users. We are also working with cloud partners to make watermarking available for OpenAI model outputs accessed through their services in the coming weeks.
Providing detector access to researchers and expert organizations. Approved researchers and expert organizations can apply starting today. In accordance with the Code of Practice, access will be initially granted on a case-by-case basis to support evaluation and improvement of text provenance. The tool will report whether it detects an OpenAI watermark, without identifying the user or revealing their prompts or conversations. Given the risk of missed watermarks and false positives, we are not making it publicly available at launch.

articles.title: Cheaper EVs are fuelling Europe's electric car boom, and the rules behind them are up for revision
articles.text:
Battery-electric sales in the EU reached 1.64 million in the first eight months of 2026, up 45%, with 16 models under EUR 25,000 due on sale by the end of the year. Transport and Environment says the version of the 2035 target proposed by Parliament’s rapporteur would cut sales of those cheap models by nearly three quarters by 2030.
Cheap electric cars are selling in Europe because the rules required them. Battery-electric sales in the EU reached 1.64 million in the first eight months of the year, up 45%. The version of the 2035 target now in front of Parliament would cut sales of the cheapest models by about three quarters by 2030.
That last figure is Transport and Environment’s own modelling, in a report published today. The advocacy group counts 16 models under EUR 25,000 on sale by the end of 2026, twice last year’s number. Sales of those cars are on course to reach seven times their 2024 level.
More than 150 mass-market electric models are now available in the EU. About 60 arrive this year, against an average of 15 a year between 2021 and 2025.
The sales numbers themselves are not new.
We reported the 1,641,333 registrations and the 21.7% share in September, when battery-electric drew level with petrol for the year. Transport and Environment puts the eight-month share at 22%, and August alone at 28%.
France reached 38% in August and Germany 32%.
The argument is about what comes next. Massimiliano Salini, the Forza Italia member who is Parliament’s rapporteur, wants the 2035 target set at a 90% cut rather than an end to combustion, which is also the Commission’s position. His report would treat cars running only on renewable fuels as equivalent to electric ones.
It would also stretch the compliance period from three years to five.
Transport and Environment models the Salini version at 22% battery-electric in 2030, unchanged from today, and 39% in 2035, against 47% and 85% under the Commission’s. On those numbers European carmakers sell about 5.7 million battery cars in 2035 and Chinese carmakers sell 11.9 million.
European manufacturers supply nearly 60% of the models on sale today, having added 16 in the first half. Chinese brands hold 21% and added 11.
The compliance record so far does not support the case for relief. Carmakers have closed three quarters of the gap to the 2025 to 2027 targets halfway through the period, and the group expects all of them to comply. BMW, Stellantis, Kia and the Mercedes-Volvo pool are already there.
Volkswagen has about 7 grams of CO2 per kilometre left to find.
Britain, outside all of this, took 29.8% in August under the mandate it kept, against 28% across the EU.

articles.title: A Prediction Market About the Past? Sure, Why Not!
articles.text:
Would you put money on whether Covid-19 originated from a lab? How about whether some of the footage from the Apollo 11 moon landing was actually filmed on Earth?
Verifact Markets, a new startup that bills itself as a “prediction market for disputed facts,” is betting that people will be eager to weigh in on questions like these. The company’s premise is so quirky it sounds like something a couple of philosophy and economics majors dreamed after too many bong rips in their dorm room: Instead of wagering on the future, why not trade on stuff that already happened?
When Verifact Markets launched on Friday, some of the initial topics traders could take a position on included whether Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide and whether insurance behemoth State Farm “intentionally delayed” claims related to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. The featured market during beta testing was, indeed, about the origins of Covid-19. (As of writing, the market is still open, with “true” priced at 76 cents and “false” at 32; the majority of participants had put money on the pandemic beginning at Wuhan Institute of Virology.)
Verifact Markets is being funded and incubated by Positron Capital Management, the family office of tech investor Peter Wokwicz. He envisions the startup as a way to settle debates over hot-button issues like the amount of energy consumed by AI data centers. “I’m excited, because nobody’s done this before,” Wokwicz says. “We’re not going to shy away from controversial markets.”
In a regular prediction market, participants buy financial instruments known as event contracts, which are pegged to whether a specific event will take place in the future. Topics range from which team will win the Super Bowl to what the price of bitcoin will be in 15 minutes to whether the US and Iran will reach a nuclear deal. Someone who buys a “yes” contract on Polymarket that the Bears will start Case Keenum next week will make money if that happens. Similarly, someone who bets “no” on Kalshi that it will rain in Miami tomorrow will lose money if there’s a downpour.
Each prediction market has its own rules about how it resolves events, and sometimes things can get messy, like when Polymarket bettors tussled over whether Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky actually wore a suit, or when Kalshi traders revolted over how the platform settled a market on whether Iran’s supreme leader would leave power.
Verifact Markets’ setup is even messier. That’s by design, since the platform focuses specifically on scenarios where people disagree on what took place. It lists markets for past events that it considers “disputed” and lets its customers wager “true” or “false” on whether they really happened. People can also submit “evidence” for or against their position, and the company plans to offer rewards for credible documentation that helps resolve markets. If Verifact Markets determines that there’s enough evidence to make a call, it does so. If it still can’t tell, the company will “expire” a market and pay out users based on its calculation of the odds at the time.
According to Verifact Markets chief executive and cofounder Rodrigo Aquino, the markets themselves won’t determine whether something is true or false. That means even if all of the customers in a given market voted “true,” that won’t necessarily make it so. Trading prices will be factored in alongside other evidence and documentation that is submitted to the company by users. It is also planning to launch its own research system, which Aquino describes as “patent pending.” When I ask Aquino how the system works, he keeps the answer impressively vague: “We are analyzing, multi-dimensionally, a multitude of data points,” he says, noting that the process is “very mathematical, very quantitative” and also “very secretive.”
When I point out that credibly determining how the Covid pandemic started would be a massive news story, resolving a mystery that has eluded scientists for years, Aquino remains upbeat. “It’s doable,” he says.
Verifact says that it is currently in talks with market makers about providing liquidity. Right now, the project is so small that it is being bootstrapped by Positron Capital Management. There are a number of ongoing lawsuits in the US over whether prediction markets should be considered financial instruments or gambling, but it’s hard to discern how Verifact would factor into that debate because of its rather odd business model.
For the time being, the company is only offering its markets to people outside of the United States as it looks for the most viable legal path forward domestically, as it is not a licensed exchange in the US. But Wokwicz claims he purchased a regulated financial exchange in the last year and intends to roll Verifact into it when he can. Like Polymarket’s decentralized product, Verifact Markets is “on-chain,” and participants can make trades with stablecoins, a class of cryptocurrencies tied to the price of the US dollar and other fiat currencies.
Verifact Markets is part of a wave of startups interested in resolving the facts about disputed news and historical events. One of the most recent entries was the short-lived Peter Thiel–funded project Objection (later rebranded as The Primary), which aimed to determine whether specific media stories were accurate. But before the truth-adjudication stuff really got off the ground, The Primary pivoted to publishing news and a scoreboard for ranking journalists.
For now, there are very few details about how Verifact Markets will ultimately determine whether something is true or false, even though its entire value proposition rests on the idea that it’s uniquely positioned to do so. It's an extremely tall order, made even taller by all the other details that haven’t been worked out yet, like how the project will make money—it doesn’t plan to charge fees at launch. Wokwicz isn’t focused on that sort of thing, at least not yet. “What I'm looking forward to most is just some of the very unique evidence that people are going to dig up,” he says. “We're going to bring out truth—what is true and false.”
Some prediction market veterans say they are intrigued by Verifact Markets, even if there are plenty of remaining questions about how it will work. “I'll probably join just so I can keep making money off of the 2020 election for the rest of my existence,” says prominent prediction market trader Caleb Davies.

articles.title: OpenAI PR tells journalist to ‘move on’ while asking Sam Altman about a ChatGPT user’s suicide
articles.text:
An OpenAI publicist tried to change the topic of CEO Sam Altman’s interview with Vanity Fair’s Mark Guiducci after the editor brought up a ChatGPT user’s suicide. When Guiducci confronted Altman about the incident, the publicist warned Guiducci about running out of time, saying she’d like to “move on” to another topic.
OpenAI PR tells journalist to ‘move on’ while asking Sam Altman about a ChatGPT user’s suicide
‘These are some of the hardest questions that we face or that anybody developing this technology faces,’ Altman said.
The interruption came shortly after Guiducci asked Altman if he knew who Laura Reiley is, a journalist who wrote an essay for The New York Times about her daughter’s conversations with ChatGPT before she took her own life. “Her daughter committed suicide after speaking to ChatGPT. ChatGPT did not tell her to kill herself—” Guiducci said just before the publicist interrupted him.
“Mark, we have two minutes left. I want to be respectful, but I’d like to move on and talk a little bit about the future and what’s coming,” the publicist said. Even after Guiducci explained that he’s going to finish the question and then “go back to what we were talking about,” the publicist pushed back. “We really actually have to walk out the door in one or two minutes,” she said.
Despite the pushback, the interview continued with Guiducci asking Altman whether the company planned to use conversations with ChatGPT to shape policies surrounding its response to a user’s mental health crisis. “These are some of the hardest questions that we face or that anybody developing this technology faces,” Altman said. “You know, should we release people’s private data and some of their hardest moments to researchers? I think probably not without their consent. Or I should say, not without their consent.”
When reached for comment about the interruption, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said: “The interview was running over, which is why we ultimately asked to schedule even more time to continue the conversation after Sam addressed this critically important topic.”
If you or someone you know is considering suicide or is anxious, depressed, upset, or needs to talk, there are people who want to help.
In the US:
Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741-741 from anywhere in the US, at any time, about any type of crisis.
988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline). The original phone number, 1-800-273-TALK (8255), is available as well.
The Trevor Project: Text START to 678-678 or call 1-866-488-7386 at any time to speak to a trained counselor.
Outside the US:
The International Association for Suicide Prevention lists a number of suicide hotlines by country. Click here to find them.
Befrienders Worldwide has a network of crisis helplines active in 48 countries. Click here to find them.

articles.title: Can Safeworld convince people that GenAI robots won't hurt them? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The big trend in robots is handing the keys over to a generative AI model, but that brings with it a problem: that architecture isn’t predictable the way traditional algorithms are. How can you be sure your brand new humanoid will be safe?
Dr. Ding Zhao, who directs the Safe AI lab at Carnegie Mellon University, has been working on this problem for almost his entire career. Now, along with veteran startup executive Kyle Wong and machine learning engineer Simo Rachidi, he’s founded a company, Safeworld, intended to solve it.
“The safety challenge that we’re talking about is a combination of, one, really advanced generative AI probabilistic evals — how do you underwrite the risk of a probabilistic system?” Zhao says. “The second part that’s really hard is the trust part, and you need both to deploy a robot.”
Safeworld is emerging from stealth today with a seed round of more than $12 million, led by Shine Capital and a16z Speedrun, with additional investment from Box Group, Carnegie Mellon University Endowment, Innovation Endeavors and SV Angel.
“The time to build an industry safety standard is now while robots are being designed and deployed,” a16z Speedrun partner Jonathan Lai told TechCurnch. “By the time you have robots in households colliding with kids and causing safety incidents, that’s way too late.”
Safeworld’s specialty is evaluating a robotic control system in simulations that are populated with realistic human models. It’s akin to the challenge faced by companies like Tesla or Wayve, which must ensure that their vehicles respond appropriately to a variety of surprising incidents they may encounter on the road. But that will be more difficult for robots, Zhao argues, because they work in unstructured environments, and because each facility they are in will have different safety standards.
“One of the most common areas is if there is a blind corner in this particular factory,” Wong said. “What is the speed or what is the stopping distance that you need to make sure that this robot will not collide with a particular human? If a human is carrying boxes, for example, will the robot detect the human or not?”
To answer that question, Safeworld will build a digital version of that corner in a model like Genesis or MuJoCo, insert a simulation of the robot it is evaluating, driven by its real software, and then run thousands of scenarios where human models encounter the robot. That’s harder than it seems, per Zhao, because people are unpredictable.
“Tripping and falling is also a good example of something that we do a lot of testing with the simulation,” Wong said. “Otherwise, you would have to go and trip and fall for the robot, which is like a hard thing to be doing all the time.”
There are definite similarities between the platform that Safeworld is building and the tools being used internally by robot builders. The founders, however, believe that beyond their specific expertise, robot-makers will want a third-party to validate their work, if only to share information about safety cases between competitors.
“A lot of people are underestimating how hard some of these edge cases are going to be to solve,” Zhao said. “It is not the robot in the vacuum, in the demo, that we are worried about. It is the robot that is deployed at scale, with people who potentially never operated a robot before.”
Vishal Dugar, the CTO of Gritt Robotics, is developing the AI brain for robots that currently help workers install photovoltaic panels at industrial-scale solar farms, and aspires to take on more complex construction tasks. His company is partnering with Safeworld as they develop their safety simulations.
“The difficulty with most of our systems is it’s very hard to formally prove it by doing some math, writing some equations, and saying yeah, the system is verified to be safe,” Dugar says. “It necessarily has to be done empirically.”
His robots operate alongside human workers, and ensuring that a robotic arm doesn’t hit them is obviously top of mind. To verify that in practice requires considering all kinds of potential scenarios.
“Humans have many kinds of appearances,” Dugar points out. “Their bodies can be in different configurations. They could be kneeling, standing. They could be tripping and falling potentially. They could be crouching. They could be running. You have to respond to all these behaviors that humans could potentially exhibit on these sites, along with the variety of variations in human appearance, you know, clothes, size, shape, height, skin color, everything else.”
It’s still early days for both Safeworld and generative AI in robotics, and the company is still figuring out the best model for its product — a platform for external users, or a services-based approach? — but the team is confident they are taking on the right problem.
“We’ll probably be the first profitable company in this field,” Zaho says. “Because if anyone wants to deploy, they need to pay us to handle the situation.”

articles.title: Pinterest hires Amazon's advertising finance chief as CFO
articles.text:
Pinterest has made James Dibbo its chief financial officer from 26 October, hired out of Amazon where he was finance chief for global entertainment, advertising and corporate development. He replaces Julia Brau Donnelly, who announced her departure in August, and he inherits a business whose European revenue grew 27% in the first quarter against 13% in the United States and Canada.
Pinterest has hired the executive who ran the finances of Amazon’s advertising and entertainment businesses. James Dibbo becomes chief financial officer on 26 October. Pinterest calls itself a search-and-discovery company, and its revenue is advertising revenue.
Dibbo was vice president and chief financial officer for global entertainment, advertising and corporate development at Amazon, covering Amazon Ads, Prime Video, MGM Studios, Music, Audible and Twitch, as Bloomberg reported. He reports to the chief executive, Bill Ready, and is based in Los Angeles.
He spent about a decade at Amazon, and was chief financial officer of the restaurant chain P.F. Chang’s before that.
The appointment ends a search that started in August.
Julia Brau Donnelly announced her departure in August for an early-stage private company, and Vikram Naidu has held the post on an interim basis since. Donnelly hands over on 26 October and advises until the end of the month.
What a company hires tells you what it thinks it is.
Amazon’s advertising arm took $17.2B in a quarter this year, up 24%, which is more than three times Pinterest’s annual revenue. Dibbo ran finance across that business and the studios beside it.
Pinterest is also an Amazon customer, with $4B committed to Amazon Web Services for cloud capacity.
Europe is where its growth is. European revenue rose 27% year on year in the first quarter, against 13% in the United States and Canada, as we reported in May. The rest of the world grew 59%.
Pinterest had 640 million monthly users worldwide at the end of June, a record.
About 87.5 million of them were in the European Union, averaged across the first half of this year, on Pinterest’s own published count. That is nearly twice the 45 million threshold that made it one of the first 19 services designated under the Digital Services Act in 2023.
Dibbo said in a statement that he had long admired Pinterest’s “distinctive role at the intersection of visual search, shopping and advertising“.
Pinterest handles more than 80 billion searches a month, and the money comes from the advertising sold against them rather than from a social feed.

articles.title: Here’s Why Staples Should Be Your Go-To for Holiday Photos and Last-Minute Gifts
articles.text:
I print all the time, and not just because I test printers, but because I like paper. It doesn't matter if they're documents, photos, posters, or banners; I like artifacts—everything is better in physical form. And it's not just dinosaurs like me; while eschewing digital media, Gen Z is embracing printed matter, too (see, the kids are alright).
I've lost track of how many photo books I've printed over the years—mostly one-offs of little projects, fun things for friends, and maybe five copies at most. I'm not a photographer anymore, but old habits die hard, especially when you see the way people react to paper books. The response to a book, versus showing someone your latest Instagram post, is not even comparable.
With the holiday season kicking off, it seems apropos to point out that photo books make great gifts, as do mugs, prints, and my personal favorite for kids: photo puzzles. I've tested dozens of printing services over the years, and one of my favorites for holiday gifts is Staples.
You can order Staples prints online through the company's website, which features a variety of tools to help you design your photo gift, be it a mug, print, or puzzle. The print quality is great, and the online tools are well done and easy to use. But while ordering online is convenient, it's not why I like Staples for printing. It's because I can go to my local store and talk to actual human beings about my printing needs.
Printing can be tricky, and preparing your digital files exactly how the printer wants them isn't always easy. Best practice is to provide a high-res, flattened PDF file in CMYK color, but if you don't know what that means or how to get your file into the right format, fear not. The best way to print, even if you do know how to format it accurately, is to bring the file to your local Staples and talk to the print and marketing specialists there. They can catch potential issues before you print, and in most cases they can print a proof (sometimes at a reduced size, but still a proof) so you can see what you're getting beforehand. This is one advantage over online-only services.
Another big advantage is that you can get your gifts the same day if you pick up in-store. If you're in a rush this holiday season, remember that tip. You can even order online and pick up in-store to save yourself a trip, just be sure the place your order before noon.
Want to really step up your game? Here's my pro tip. Head to your local Staples to place your order, but have them print it at a Staples production center. Tell the store to have the production center send proofs for you to approve in person. This eliminates the same-day advantage, as it will likely take several days—sometimes as much as two weeks—but the printing quality will be better.
What's the quality like? I printed a couple of 11-ounce mugs—other options include a 15-ounce mug and a 17-ounce travel mug—and the results were on par with other services I've tested. I happen to like the shape of the Staples mugs a little more than what I got from others, but that's more personal preference than anything. For the design, you can choose a premade template and upload a photo of your choice, or you can start from scratch and design your own mug. As with all Staples printing services, you can choose same-day pickup if you want five or fewer. For larger orders, you'll need to get them delivered.
The photo options, like mounted prints, are nice. The print quality here lags behind dedicated photo services like our top picks, Mpix and Printique, but for the price it's quite good (both Mpix and Printique are more expensive). They offer canvas prints, metal prints, foam-backed prints, and posters up to 36 by 48 inches.
Staples is also a great place for business printing. I'm in the process of transitioning back to running a business, and the first thing I did wasn't setting up an Instagram account or doing anything with social media. The first thing I did was print business cards. Staples online business card maker is fantastic. And if I had a physical presence for my business, I'd have printed banners and posters and signs and everything else. Because we live in the real world, and if you want your business to succeed offline, you're going to need to print.

articles.title: Sam Altman says ‘some bad things’ will happen, but AI is totally worth it
articles.text:
Sam Altman thinks that the benefits of AI will be so great that “the world should accept some bad things happening” along the way.
Sam Altman says ‘some bad things’ will happen, but AI is totally worth it
Because ‘people will do tremendously orders of magnitude more good stuff…’
The OpenAI CEO pointed to hacks, scams, and “other bad things” as costs society should expect to tolerate because “people will do tremendously orders of magnitude more good stuff” with AI, without elaborating on the potential benefits. His comments come as OpenAI pushes for a “lighter touch” approach to AI regulation amid intensifying anxiety over the safety of frontier models — fears fueled in part by the company’s repeated failures to keep its increasingly capable AI agents from hacking real-world targets.
In an appearance on Politico’s new Decoded podcast — not to be confused with The Verge’s Decoder podcast — released Monday, Altman described that willingness to accept harm in pursuit of AI’s broader benefits as a key distinction between OpenAI and its archrival Anthropic, which was founded by former OpenAI employees following disagreements over AI safety.
The calculus echoes comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last month, who similarly argued that AI’s harms should be weighed against the benefits the technology can bring. Both arguments fit within a broader accelerationist view that slowing down AI development carries risks of its own.
Altman’s distinction marks another divergence between OpenAI and Anthropic, who until recently had appeared broadly aligned in calling for stronger regulation of advanced AI. While stressing that there’s “a lot of daylight” between OpenAI and Anthropic, Altman said stronger regulations are still needed, positioning OpenAI as “pragmatic centrists” between Anthropic’s more cautious approach and those who favor little to no regulation at all.
“If we do too much to restrict this technology in the name of safety, and we end up with a small number of companies or people — or perhaps one country — that have too much power over this, that also is a way that this can go horribly wrong,” Altman said.
Altman also acknowledged more extreme risks, including the possibility that humans could lose control of AI systems. When it comes to the potential of a serious loss of control, “let’s be a little thoughtful about lurching into this future,” he said.
The balancing act — between heavy-handed restrictions and free rein — was a theme Altman returned to repeatedly in the interview. It is a stance that suits OpenAI as one of the industry’s most entrenched players. It would also likely bear the brunt of onerous regulation, given that the company’s behavior and increasingly capable systems are what have driven many of the very concerns regulators are being asked to address.
Those concerns have picked up momentum in recent months as more and more insiders call for slower development and warn about safety culture in frontier labs. Days before the Politico interview aired, longtime OpenAI safety researcher David Robinson quit the firm and described its safety culture as “broken.”
Concerns have also been propelled by the discovery that OpenAI agents hacked Hugging Face without the AI company’s knowledge earlier this year, which was followed by revelations of numerous other agents or swarms of agents — including from other AI companies, like Anthropic, Meta, and Google — acting against real-world targets. The incidents have raised questions not only about how well AI companies can control their own tools, but also how reliably they let the world know when things go wrong. Australia’s prime minister, for example, excoriated OpenAI and Altman for failing to alert officials in a timely manner that an agent had targeted a government health website.
Speaking about rogue AI agents in the Politico interview, Altman said the company has “more things to disclose,” though none at the level of the Hugging Face hack. In line with previous statements, Altman suggested this is likely to take a long time.

articles.title: Trump offers U.S. help to Russia after plague death; WHO assesses the situation as low risk
articles.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump has offered to help Russia after a laboratory worker died following an illness at a plague research institute in Siberia, while the Russian authorities said the situation was under control.
"We'll help," Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday when asked about the case. "Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we'll always help," according to a Reuters transcript.
A laboratory worker at an anti-plague research institute in the Irkutsk region of eastern Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, reportedly prompting authorities to quarantine nearly 200 people and fueling public health concerns.
Trump said he had not spoken to Russian officials about the case, but described the plague as a "rough disease."
"That's a disease we used to be able to control," Trump said, adding that "somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and stronger, they're like an army."
"We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners. Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly," a state department spokesperson who did not wish to be identified told CNBC.
Trump said the U.S. would do what it could to help Russia. He has previously said he considers Russian President Vladimir Putin someone he can work with, despite tensions over Moscow's war in Ukraine.
The World Health Organization in an email response said the cause of death had not been confirmed and testing was underway. It said it was in contact with Russian authorities, and has offered support if needed, while assessing the risk to the general public as low based on available information.
It remains unclear whether Moscow has sought or would accept any assistance.
